About Phy-Hub

Introduction

Classical physics accurately predicts the movement of objects in our everyday world. However, there are effects it does not account for, and as objects approach the speed of light, these effects, which are negligible at low speeds, become increasingly significant. This leads to two observers moving at high speeds relative to each other becoming unable to agree on the lengths of objects and the times at which events occur. Crucially though, one thing remains constant: the speed of light relative to each observer is the same, regardless of their movement. We must redefine our classical understanding of time and space to find out how this can be. This is where special relativity comes into play.

Special relativity is vital in particle physics, nuclear physics, and astrophysics, used to calculate nuclear reaction output power and measure galaxy speeds. It is also needed for precision timekeeping on fast-moving GPS satellites to accurately calculate positions.

Despite its importance, special relativity continues to confuse even those well-versed in physics and mathematics. It can be as confusing to visualize and understand as quantum mechanics is. The theory requires letting go of some deeply held intuitions about the absolute nature of space and time, which differ from our everyday experience of the physical world.

This handbook is meant to offer an intuitive, visual, and detailed overview of special relativity. The aim is to stay simple and avoid unnecessary abstraction in explanations. For example, the diagrams in this handbook represent time in one of two ways: through animations or through a storyboard of snapshot diagrams that display a timeline of events. This approach avoids the use of unnecessary space-time diagrams that represent time on one of the axes, which make special relativity more abstract and confusing to visualize.

The first chapter is readable even for those without a math or physics background. It provides a non-mathematical, visual overview of the concepts. This chapter builds an intuitive understanding of the core ideas step by step, providing a solid foundation for developing the essential mathematical framework in later sections. I drew inspiration from many resources, which includes the book "Relativity visualized" [1].

The mathematical portion will begin with deriving how space and time coordinates function in special relativity. This will be followed by velocity addition, the Doppler effect, and the energy-momentum relationship. In addition to these topics, we will also explore some interesting subjects not typically covered in standard resources. These include how a source's emitted light is concentrated in the direction of its movement, aberration, and how a delay in light signals to an observer means they are currently viewing sources of light in their past positions. These topics will probably not mean much to you yet, but they will give fascinating insights.

Now, let us begin!

Part I.
The Concepts Explained

Here, we will give an overview of the main concepts of special relativity, without the math. This is to show how special relativity works without needing to comprehend the math at the same time, as the math can distract from understanding the concepts themselves.

Chapter 1. Overview of Concepts

To make sense of special relativity, we will first look at the classical understanding of the world. Then, we will see how we must change these classical laws of physics to account for light's constant speed relative to all observers. Which in turn will lead to many interesting consequences. The chapter begins with an overview of the core concepts to help us understand why we need special relativity and what it means, leaving the mathematical details and deeper insights for the following chapters.

This chapter's concepts will establish the mathematical framework for later chapters by using physical objects, such as moving trucks on roads, to represent the perspectives of different observers. Whereas in the mathematical chapters, we will use coordinate axes to represent the different perspectives (frames of reference).

Later, you will see the parallels between this conceptual overview and the mathematical chapters. This chapter will provide an overview of all the required concepts for special relativity, building up the needed knowledge bit by bit, starting with our classical understanding of how perspectives (frames of reference) work and showing how our understanding must change if we are to allow all observers to view light as moving at the same constant speed.

1.1 Classical Addition of Velocities

Imagine a truck carrying a cannon moving at 20 meters per second, and the cannon fires a ball at 100 meters per second relative to the truck. Classically, we add the truck's speed to the ball's speed, to find that the ball moves at 120 meters per second relative to the road. So, in classical physics, velocities are directly added. The ball relative to the road would move at the speed of the ball relative to the truck plus the truck's speed relative to the road, as shown in Figure (1.1).

However, this classical understanding is just a very good approximation for objects in our everyday life that we are used to seeing, which are moving much slower than the speed of light (roughly 300,000,000 meters per second), but we will get to this later. For now, in the following sections, we will explain what an inertial reference frame is and how this works in the classical context so that you can see more clearly the differences between classical and special relativity.

1.2 Inertial Reference Frame

A reference frame is a grid of coordinates we can overlay on space, so that we can state, with respect to it, where and when an event occurs. If this grid is stationary or moving at a constant velocity, it is called an inertial reference frame. In the previous truck example, we could associate a reference frame with the truck by introducing a grid of coordinates that is stationary relative to the truck and, hence, moving along with it. This perspective, fixed to the truck, is the truck's frame of reference. A second grid of coordinates, stationary relative to the road, can also be introduced to represent the road's reference frame. These grids of coordinates are shown from the road's reference frame in Figure (1.2).

An inertial frame of reference is a reference frame that is not being accelerated. You can tell if you are being accelerated, as you will feel a force. For example, in an accelerating car, you will feel the seat accelerate into you, with your body pushing back into it. This principle is used in accelerometers to measure acceleration, as shown in Figure (1.3).

We will now look at how movement changes in classical relativity when we change between these inertial frames.

1.3 Classical Inertial Reference Frames

To see how to switch between reference frames in special relativity, we first need to introduce the classical approach.

To illustrate this, we will consider a setup with two rats on a treadmill, as shown in Figure (1.4), with three rocks hanging above the platform, which are at rest relative to the room. The two frames of reference will be the treadmill's platform and the room in which it is located. Both rats start under the same rock. One rat runs to a rock positioned in the treadmill's forward direction. The other rat runs to an equally spaced rock to the side. After this, they return to the starting rock.

Here, the platform can be seen as the medium in which the rats move. Both rats travel at the same constant speed relative to the platform, with the platform either at rest or moving more slowly than the rats, so they can reach the rocks.

If the platform is at rest, they will return to the starting rock simultaneously. But if the treadmill is on and the platform is moving, the rats will also have to work against the platform's movement to reach the rocks. This will lead to different distances the rats have to travel relative to the platform, and as a result, the rats return to the starting rock at different times. Figure (1.5) shows what the direction of movement of the rats and rocks looks like in each of the reference frames when the platform is moving.


From the room's perspective, the platform is moving backwards. The rat moving in the direction of the treadmill's motion will experience impedance to its movement from the backwards pull of the platform. But after it turns around, it will have a boost from the platform to return to the starting rock. Meanwhile, the sideways-moving rat will have to move sideways and balance out the platform's backwards pull to keep its movement in the direction of the hanging rocks. This gives different path lengths depending on the reference frame, as shown in Figure (1.5). The rats in the platform's reference frame move with the same speed for all the paths, represented by the arrows. Whereas, in the room's reference frame, we have a slower constant speed of the sideways-moving rat and two different speeds for the forward and backward paths of the other rat. This leads to different times for the rats to return to the starting rock.

The rats here use the medium of the treadmill's platform to move, and similarly, it was thought that light needed a medium, called the aether, to travel through space. If there were such a medium, we could test how fast it moved relative to Earth by measuring the difference in the return times of light emitted in two perpendicular directions, just as in the treadmill example. So, next, we will look at the notion of a universal medium, referred to as the aether, and whether we can have the same frame switching for light traveling in two different frames of reference. As we did in this section.

1.4 The Aether

In the theory of electromagnetism from the late 1800s, it was believed that light was a wave and, therefore, would need a medium that filled the vacuum of space for it to travel through, called "the luminiferous aether", and that light traveled at a constant speed relative to this aether, like how the rats in the previous section moved at a constant speed relative to the medium of the treadmill's platform. It was from the theory of electromagnetism and the experiments performed from it that showed that light should have a constant speed, at least relative to this aether, but it was yet to be known that light would actually have a constant speed relative to all things.

If the aether existed, the Earth would be moving through it, as shown in Figure (1.6).

So, an experimental setup by Michelson and Morley, shown in Figure (1.7), called an interferometer, was devised to measure Earth's movement through the aether [2] by measuring how it affected the return times of light emitted in different directions, as observed in Earth's reference frame. It did this by splitting a single light beam into two perpendicular paths, which were then reflected back to be recombined and sent toward a light detector. By rotating a platform that the setup is on, the two light paths could be aligned, one parallel and the other perpendicular to the Earth's motion through the presumed aether. They reasoned that if the speed of light were constant relative to the proposed aether, as we had for the rats in the previous section, the split light beams would recombine at different times.

From the previous section's system of rats on a treadmill, we can see that the treadmill's platform is analogous to the aether, and the rats are analogous to the light. Both have the room where these experiments are done as the other inertial reference frame.

However, when Michelson and Morley performed the experiment, they found no difference in travel time to the detector for both paths, indicating that there was no difference in the speed of light in any direction in Earth's reference frame. Hence, light's speed is not dependent on the supposed aether. This null result seriously discredited the aether theories. It led to the proposal by Einstein in 1905 that the speed of light (in a vacuum) is a universal constant, independent of the motion of the observer or the source.

To have a universal speed of light (in a vacuum), it will require us to change our ideas about how time and position are perceived by different observers.

1.5 Speed of Light

Experiments conducted in a vacuum showed that light does not just travel at a constant velocity relative to the proposed medium (the aether), but actually travels at a constant velocity relative to all reference frames. The observed speed of light is independent of how fast the source and receiver of that light are moving within the frame, as shown with a moving truck's headlights in Figure (1.8). Light moves more slowly in materials such as glass, but this is due to interactions between the light and the material, which impede its movement.

Light itself moves extremely fast compared to any other everyday speeds we are used to (roughly 300,000,000 meters per second; it can travel the world's diameter in the blink of an eye). This is why we do not notice any delay in the light from the things we see in everyday life, and we assume everything is located where we are currently seeing it, though we should remember that there is this delay. For example, the light we currently see from the sun was emitted 8 minutes ago for it to reach us now, and the further an object is located from us, the further back in time we are currently seeing it because of this delay.

When we look at the same truck setup as in Figure (1.1), but now have it in a vacuum, where the cannon firing a cannonball is swapped for headlights emitting light, we will find the same speed of light when measured relative to the truck or the road, but how can this be true?

For this to be true, we need a new way of thinking about the addition of velocities. This is because the velocities of objects must be added in a way that is consistent with the requirement that the speed of light is constant but also gives the approximate classical addition at speeds of objects at much less than the speed of light, like how we observed in the situation with the cannon and truck, shown in Figure (1.1). Since the speed of light depends only on the units of time and position, the only way to correct for this is to have the measured positions and times of objects transform differently when switching between reference frames than the classical way. This is what we will talk about next. For the curious, it was the experiment by Ole Rømer (link) that showed that light travels at a finite speed rather than being instantaneously emitted and received.

1.6 Position and Time

1.6.1 Time Dilation

Consider a simple clock, as shown in Figure (1.9), made of a light pulse moving back and forth vertically between two mirrors on a moving truck, one on the truck's floor and the other on the roof directly above it. Each tick of the clock is defined as the time it takes for the light to travel from one mirror to the other and back. For an observer in the truck, they will see the light go straight up and down between the mirrors, but an observer stationary relative to the road will see not just the light traveling up and down but also with the movement of the truck to allow it to travel back and forth between the mirrors.

Given that the distance light travels is longer in the frame with the truck moving, and that from the previous sections we know that the speed of light is the same in both reference frames, to keep the speed of light invariant, the clock itself must tick more slowly in moving objects.

How much slower time is passing in the moving truck relative to the road observer can be determined from the ratio of the lengths of the paths in each frame, as shown in Figure (1.9), which is the same ratio as the time between the ticks.

Importantly, this time dilation phenomenon isn't limited to light clocks; it applies universally to all types of clocks. If you were to play a movie on the truck, it would take longer to play through from start to finish for an observer watching it from the road's reference frame. An observer on the road and in the truck experience time at different rates. This is not just an illusion; it is a physical reality.

The closer the truck goes to the speed of light, the more significant the difference in how fast the road frame's time flows relative to the truck frame's time. This can be seen as an increasingly longer horizontal stretch in the path of the light from the perspective of someone standing still on the road, with the time between each tick approaching infinity as the truck approaches the speed of light.

You may ask about the possibility that the distance between the floor and roof of the truck becoming smaller the faster the truck is moving relative to the road, to allow for the light clock to tick at the same speed, and to get rid of the need for the time dilation, but that would actually lead to contradictions which will be shown later in figure (1.12).

Now, if we instead had two trucks moving at the same speed relative to the road but in opposite directions. Each truck would see its light moving vertically up and down with the other truck's light moving a longer diagonal path. Hence, each truck perceives the other truck's clock ticking more slowly. An observer in the road's reference frame would see both trucks move at the same speed and, hence, their diagonal paths having the same length, giving the same passage of time between ticks for both trucks. That is, the slowing of time for moving objects is the same regardless of their relative direction of motion; only the relative speed determines how far the light travels to create each tick of the clock. This concept is confusing and difficult to visualize, but it will get easier with practice.

For now, though, we will continue building up the concepts of special relativity.

1.6.2 Simultaneity

Imagine a truck in its rest frame, with a light bulb in the middle and mirrors on the front and back walls. If the light bulb emits a pulse of light, the light will travel from the center of the truck to reach the mirrors simultaneously, and also back to reach the light bulb simultaneously. An observer on the road watching the truck drive past will see the light bulb simultaneously emit light in both directions and simultaneously return to the bulb. However, the light reflects off each wall's mirrors at different times in the road's frame to do this, as shown in Figure (1.10). This is because the speed of light is the same for both directions, but the truck is moving, meaning the back of the truck is moving towards where the bulb was when the light pulse was emitted, making the distance traveled shorter. The light travels a longer distance to the front wall because the wall has moved further away from when it was emitted. Because of this, the observer on the road will see the light hit the mirrors at different times.

Consequently, the times at which events occur, such as when the light reaches either mirror, differ for observers in different reference frames. There is no one true order of events. For example, an observer in a faster-moving vehicle moving in the opposite direction would see the light reach the front wall first. However, for all observers, the light will return to the central light bulb simultaneously. If two events occur at the same position simultaneously, then they occur simultaneously in all frames of reference. This means the light returns to the center of the light bulb simultaneously in each frame.

A note here is that we are talking about when the events actually happen in each frame, not when the light from those events reaches the observer, which is later due to the time it takes the light from an event to travel to the observer for them to see it. Also, I have left out any mention of the length contraction of the truck, which will be introduced in the next section, and why it must be equal in both directions from the lightbulb for the all the light to return to the light bulb simultaneously.

1.6.3 Length Contraction

Consider a truck, in its rest frame, carrying a square container. If a light bulb at the square container's center emits light in the two horizontal directions and the two vertical directions, it will bounce off the mirrored sides of the truck and return to the center simultaneously. We require that, in the moving frame, they also return to the center simultaneously, as multiple events that occur at a single point simultaneously in one frame, must occur simultaneously in all other frames. The light reflects off the walls at different locations, so the order of reflections in time will depend on the observer, as described in the previous section. The time between the light being emitted and absorbed from the light bulb is the dilated time, as described in section (1.6.1).

To achieve this simultaneity in the return of the light to the bulb, the total length of the path of light in each of the four directions must be the same, as light's speed is the same in all directions. We can determine the length of the up and down path from the time dilation section (1.6.1), and this is the length the path needs to be in the horizontal directions as well. The paths can only have this length if the truck is contracted in the direction of its motion, to allow for the light to be reflected from the walls at the required positions for these path lengths. The amount of contraction is the same in both directions. The exact amount of the contraction can be worked out geometrically, and it turns out that the ratio of the increase in the amount of time that passes before the light is reabsorbed is inversely proportional to the amount the truck is contracted in the direction of its movement. That is, if in a moving frame the time is dilated so that the light clock takes twice as long between ticks, then the length of the moving truck is half its length at rest. This is shown in the following figure.

We now know that moving objects must shrink in the direction they move to allow for a consistent speed of light in each frame. But this shrinking is not noticeable when objects move much slower than the speed of light. If you are unsatisfied with this, the next section will explain the need for length contraction in another way using three accelerating cars. But first, we will look at the reason we did not consider any change in the sizes of moving objects in the directions perpendicular to an object's movement.

If we consider the possibility that a moving object contracts in the direction perpendicular to its motion, we find that this leads to contradictions, as shown in figure (1.12). As it allows for the possibility that a moving object's size in the perpendicular direction is smaller than a container (that is moving relative to the object) when observed in the container's rest frame, but larger than its container in the object's frame. This is impossible, as this would break the container just because you decided to view the object from a different reference frame.

In the previous section, in the frame with the truck moving, we saw that the emitted light reaches the top and bottom of the square container at the same time. But the times it reaches the left and right walls are not simultaneous, and it is this difference in timings that allows the truck to contract in the direction of movement without the contradictions that arise when we consider contraction in the perpendicular direction to the movement.

Another Illustration of Length Contraction

Suppose we have three cars, equally spaced, and at rest on the road, as shown in Figure (1.13). If the middle car emits a pulse of light, it will reach the front and back car simultaneously for the road observer and the car's observers. When it reaches them both, all the cars accelerate for a predetermined fixed amount of time to the same speed. Following this acceleration period, the cars have maintained equal spacing relative to both the car observers and the observer on the road. As for all observers, the light reached the front and back cars at the same time.

Now, suppose we do this a second time, with the middle car releasing another pulse. In this case, within the frame of the observers in the cars, we again see the front and back drivers receive the pulses simultaneously, meaning that they will start accelerating at the same time. After the acceleration has finished, the distances between the cars will be the same for the car observers. But for the road observer, they see the back car receive the signal first, as that car is moving towards the point where the light pulse was emitted, and the front car is moving away from it. This would mean the back car would accelerate first, getting closer to the front car before the front car begins to accelerate to that same final speed that the back car has already reached. This results in the cars being closer together after the acceleration. The observers in the car and the road observer disagree about what the distances between the cars are. This contraction of length between cars, in the road's frame in which the cars are moving, is called Lorentz length contraction, which means that objects that are moving faster become shorter, and the distances between the objects also become shorter.

1.7 Doppler Effect

If we have a light source at rest, emitting circular pulses of light with equal time intervals between each pulse, we will get concentric circular pulses in this frame. But if we move to a frame in which the source is moving to the right, each circular pulse is emitted from a different position. Due to the source moving, each pulse will be emitted closer to the right-hand side of the previous pulses, creating a bunching of the pulses (increase in frequency) in the direction of movement and a spreading out (decrease in frequency) in the opposite direction. This also happens in the classical version of the Doppler effect. For example, you will notice that an ambulance or police car sounds different when driving towards or away from you, due to the bunching up and spreading of sound waves in the direction and opposite direction of the moving vehicle. However, in special relativity, we must also account for the time dilation of the pulses, which will give a longer time between each subsequent pulse. This is due to objects moving relative to an observer, and therefore having their perceived time moving more slowly. This is called the second-order Doppler effect, most notably seen in optical clocks. It has a decreasing effect on the frequency in all directions. However, in the direction of the source's movement, this is outweighed by the frequency increase from the previous bunching-up effect. Since the energy of the light is proportional to the frequency, it is also increased in the direction of motion of the source due to the Doppler effects and decreased in the opposite direction.


One thing not mentioned yet in this picture is that the light is also affected by a phenomenon called aberration, which changes the angular distribution of the light at each part of the spherical pulses. This will be explained in the next section.

1.8 Aberration

Here, we will talk about what the Doppler effect in the previous section has yet to show, which is the effect on the angular distribution of the light in each part of the spherical pulses. We will show that there is a higher concentration of light in the direction of the source's movement, as shown in Figure (1.15).

With the help of the length contraction section (1.6.3), Consider a truck with a spherically mirrored container, with a central bulb that emits light in all directions. In the rest frame, all light reaches the spherical wall simultaneously and returns to the center bulb simultaneously. Then, in the moving frame, the spherical container's length contracts, and the light moves at the same speed, reflecting off the same parts of the walls but at different times, and then returns to the center bulb simultaneously. For this to be true, the light must be aberrated (have their direction of propagation changed), as shown in the diagram, to allow for the simultaneous return to the bulb.


From the diagrams, you can see how the direction of light's propagation is changed when emitted or absorbed by a moving source relative to its rest frame. This is called relativistic aberration. The faster the source is moving, the more the direction of each part of the light pulse is aberrated.

If the speed of a source were to approach the speed of light, all emitted light's propagation direction would approach the direction of movement of the source. If the source could theoretically reach the speed of light, all light would be emitted in the direction of the source, but also move at the same speed. That is, the source would move with the emitted light, and it would not leave the vicinity of the source. The rate at which it emits the light would also tend to zero. If a photon theoretically had mass and its influence on the gravitational force moved at the speed of light, then we would not be able to feel any gravitational effects from this theoretical photon with mass outside its vicinity. This is due to all its gravitational field being propagated in the direction of its movement and at the same speed as the photon.

Now, let us look at how the aberration effect is used when astronomers map the stars in the sky.

1.9 Aberration When Observing the Stars

Earth's view of the universe is distorted differently by the aberration effect, depending on which direction the Earth is currently moving in its orbit around the Sun. This needs to be taken into account when making observations with telescopes, so that we get the locations of stars that agree with measurements when the Earth is moving in different directions.

To get the locations of the stars that are consistent throughout the year, astronomers can calculate the direction of the received light in the rest frame of the sun instead of the Earth, as the sun's movement is more consistent. This is shown in the following diagram.


The sun is also moving relative to the Milky Way galaxy it is orbiting. Therefore, you could go a step further and always calculate the light's direction with respect to the center of the galaxy.

Now, we will look at the combination of the Doppler effect and aberration in the next section.

1.10 Relativistic Beaming

When the Doppler effect and relativistic aberration are combined, it is known as relativistic beaming. If we have a source in its rest frame emitting a spherical pulse of light with evenly distributed angles. Then in a second frame with the source now moving, the Doppler effect has the spherical pulse's wavelength bunched up in the direction of movement (giving a change in the color of the light), with the aberrational effect also giving the angular spread of the light at a higher concentration in the direction of the movement of the source, as shown in figures (1.17).



In astrophysics, they need to account for beaming when observing distant stars that are moving relative to us, so they can accurately calculate their brightness and the spectrum of light they emit, among other things. We also need to consider that the position we are currently seeing the stars in is their past position, due to the delay in light reaching us on Earth, which is referred to as the retarded position. We will talk about this next.

1.11 A Source's Retarded Field of Light

We can make a vector field plot, which shows the position and direction of light in space as arrows. So if we have a source in its rest frame that continually emits light pulses with a constant time interval between them, we get what is shown in Figure (1.19.a). If we wanted to know what this light vector field looked like in a frame where the source is moving, we would need to account for the fact that the position from which the source emitted each pulse, is its past position (retarded position). We also have the dilated time between pulses in this moving frame, so using these and the beaming effect from the previous section, we get the light's vector field as shown in Figure (1.19.b). From this, we can work out the distribution and, hence, the concentration of the light for any moving source relative to when it is at rest. If you look closely at the diagrams, you will see the aberrated rings of all the pulses, all with different points from which they were emitted, with them being more compact in the direction of the source's movement.


In particle physics, the photon is the particle that composes light. It is the carrier of the electromagnetic force between charges. So, how the light's propagation transforms when switching between frames is necessary to understand electromagnetism, and how the magnetic field comes about for moving sources. The diagram of the moving source shows where the source and the light currently are. But, if you were an observer at a particular position in the vector field, you would see the source at its retarded position and not where it currently is, as the light has to travel to you before you see it. This will be used in the next section to show that you can perceive things moving faster than light, even if they are not.

1.12 Velocity

We looked at how velocities at the speed of light change between different frames of reference, that is, how their directions of propagation are rotated (aberrated). However, for objects moving at velocities slower than that of light, their speed will change in addition to the direction being transformed when switching between frames. This is because we need the relativistic transform to approach the classical transform as we consider lower and lower speeds of objects. To understand the general velocity transformation, some mathematical detail is needed, so we will brush over this for now and instead look at how the apparent velocities of objects can be more than the speed of light, even if they are actually moving more slowly.

1.13 Apparent versus Actual Velocity

Imagine that a ball one light year away (the distance it takes light to travel in a year) is fired directly towards you, as shown in Figure (1.20). It will take one year for the first light from when the ball starts moving to reach you. If the ball moves at three-quarters of the speed of light, it will hit you in four-thirds of a year (a year and four months) after it is fired. The last light from the ball will reach you just as the ball hits you. As you perceive it, the time between the first and last light from the moving ball is four months. During those four months, you will see the ball start at its initial position and travel a distance of one light-year. So, to you, the ball appears to have been moving three times faster than light. This is just how it appears to the observer due to the delay in the light signal, giving the latency in how the system is observed.

This shows how important it is to account for the delay in light from objects when observing relativistic systems. This view is called the delayed/retarded view, meaning that what we see now are objects in their past positions, and the further away objects are from us, the further into the past we are currently seeing them.

1.14 Summary

A key early concept was that light traveled through a medium called the luminiferous aether. The Michelson-Morley experiment attempted to measure Earth's motion relative to this aether. Surprisingly, no difference in the speed of light was found through this proposed aether in any direction. This conflicted with the intuitive addition of velocities, discredited the aether theory, and led Einstein to propose that light travels at a constant speed in all inertial frames of reference as a fundamental principle.

Special relativity emerged from this insight that light's speed in a vacuum is constant for all observers, regardless of the light source's speed relative to each observer. This required rethinking the concepts of time intervals and distances between points to accommodate light's fixed speed. It led to the requirement that a clock moving relative to an observer ticks more slowly from the observer's perspective while also being contracted in the direction of its motion. This was shown in Figure (1.9) and Figure (1.11). The faster an object moves relative to an observer, the more its length contracts and its time dilates to the observer.

It also led to the simultaneity of events not being absolute. For example, light emitted from the middle of a moving truck reaches the front and back walls simultaneously for an observer at rest in the truck. But an observer standing still on the road sees the light hit both walls at different times, as shown in Figure (1.10). There is no universal "now" at a distance-observers relate times of events differently. It is only events that occur simultaneously at the same location, that occur simultaneously in all frames of reference.

Classical physics is verified by our day-to-day experience, though this does not reflect the full reality, as relativistic effects only become readily noticeable at speeds close to that of light. With the speed of light being 300,000,000 meters per second, astronomically faster than what we experience in our daily lives.

When it comes to velocities, they combine differently than in classical physics. However, we must ensure that the transforms reduce to the intuitive addition of velocities of classical physics at low speeds while accommodating light's constant rate in all frames of reference. This leads to initially bizarre outcomes, such as apparent faster-than-light motion, which arises due to the delay in light signals from objects at a distance. Nevertheless, special relativity gives a truer, more accurate picture of reality.

Due to space-time effects on wave propagation, we also have seen that the emitted light's frequencies shift (Doppler effect) for a moving source, and that light is concentrated in the direction of the source's motion (aberrational effect). Together, these effects both focus light in the direction of moving sources. This effect is called relativistic beaming.

These effects will all be explained more fully with math in the coming chapters, along with other effects that require the math to fully understand, as well as new energy, mass, and momentum conservation laws. We will derive everything step by step, starting with the transformation of positions and times between reference frames.

< Previous Next >

Part II.
The Essential Concepts Derived

Here, we will go through the mathematical details of the essential concepts of special relativity, all derived step by step. The chapters in this part teach the basics of special relativity. When taught at university, it typically makes up only a part of one module in the first year and is taught over 2–3 weeks. The topics in this part will be taught during this time.

Chapter 2. Position, Time, and Velocity

Now that we have learned about the concepts of special relativity, we can use them and let the mathematics begin. Starting with classical relativity, which will give us an understanding of how to transform coordinates between reference frames. We can then later compare the special relativistic coordinate transforms to this classical transform to help with our intuition.

What we learn here will be directly used in all the following chapters to derive more foundational concepts of the theory, as everything else is built upon this chapter, which explains how positions and times are transformed between two inertial frames to keep the speed of light constant.

In this chapter, we will begin by looking at how switching between two inertial frames was done classically. Then, we will use two postulates (foundational assumptions) as the basis for special relativity, and by following the reasoning from the previous chapter, we will learn how to switch between frames in special relativity. That is, we will first derive the time dilation and length contraction equations, so that we can then find the full transform of the space and time coordinates between two inertial frames. In doing so, we will encounter a very useful quantity, which we will denote as γ (gamma). This quantity will be used throughout this book to simplify equations. Lastly, we will look at the transform for infinitesimal (tiny) changes in distances and use this to derive how velocities and accelerations change when switching between two inertial frames. By the end of this chapter, you will understand coordinate transforms between two frames, both conceptually and mathematically. You will also understand the velocity and acceleration transforms, and how to derive them.

2.1 Classical Relativity

Classical (Galilean) relativity was the previous theory of how to transform coordinates to different inertial frames. In many situations in physics, it is a good enough approximation and is still used as the standard.

It was based on two assumptions: In each frame, you observe the following;

  • The distance between objects is the same.

  • Time flows at the same rate in each frame, and therefore, the time that an event occurs is the same in each frame.

These two statements will be the basis for our derivations.

So let us see how the mathematics works for the classical transform of position and time coordinates between two inertial observers' frames, by looking at the coordinates of an event in an initial reference frame with a second inertial frame's coordinate axis moving relative to the initial frame's, illustrated in Figure (2.1):

As shown in the diagram, we are in the initial frame with origin o― defined by coordinates (0,0,0), and the primed frame is moving in the z-direction at velocity v such that the position of the primed origin relative to the initial frame's axis is

(2.1)oo′→=(0,0,vt)

at time t from when the origins overlapped. If there is an event at position

(2.2)r―=(x,y,z)

the event is described by

(2.3)e―=(x,y,z,t)

Then, in the primed frame, we will have the event described by the primed coordinates that we want to transform into, as

(2.4)e―′=(x′,y′,z′,t′)

To switch into the primed frame's coordinates, we need to recall from the previous assumptions that distances and times are conserved, and therefore the length and directions of all the vectors between o―, o―′ and e― are the same in each frame, and time flows at the same rate (t′=t), from this knowledge and Figure (2.1) we have the event's coordinates described in the primed frame by its coordinate axis as

(2.5)r―′=(x′,y′,z′)=r―−oo′→=(x,y,z−vt)

This equation gives us the full description of the position and time transform for an event as

(2.6)x′=xy′=yz′=z−vtat time: t′=t

These are the equations that define classical relativity. We can compare these to the equations of the coordinate transforms in special relativity later. They define the event's position relative to the axis of whichever frame that we are in. The special relativistic equations we will derive later will look similar to these, but with a few extra factors.

We can also write the initial frame's event coordinates in terms of the primed coordinates, by rearranging the transformation equations, giving the inverse transform as

(2.7)x=x′y=y′z=z′+vt′at time: t=t′

So the inverse transformation, going from the primed frame to the original, is just a matter of swapping all primed and initial coordinates and changing the sign on the frame velocity. This can be seen at time t=0 when we have the frame's origins overlapping, as we have the freedom to choose either frame to be the original, as no frame is particularly special, and depending on which one you pick, the relative velocity is either v or-v. We will have the same rules in special relativity later on when we want to get the inverse transform.

You might have noticed that the direction of the second frame is in the upward z-direction, rather than to the right like it is in the truck diagrams from the previous chapter. This is to help us later when we use spherical polar coordinates and to help us see the symmetries. But that is a couple of chapters away; for now, we will look at the assumptions of special relativity and their consequences, which we will then apply to the same notion of an event that we have in Figure (2.1).

2.2 Postulates of Special Relativity

For classical relativity, we started with two assumptions. It turns out these assumptions need to be thrown away, as they contradict the experimental evidence that the speed of light is constant regardless of the motion of the observer or light's source. We replace these assumptions with two new ones, called the postulates of special relativity:

  1. The speed of light in a vacuum is the same in all inertial/non-accelerating frames of reference.

  2. The laws of physics and the outcome of experiments are the same in all inertial frames of reference. If an observer in an inertial reference frame were to carry out an experiment, they would find the same result if they had carried it out within a different inertial frame instead.

The first postulate here will be the most important for deriving the transform equations of special relativity. It will be used to show how time is dilated (slowed down) for moving objects. The second postulate has the consequence that if events occur simultaneously at an overlapping position in one frame, then they will also occur simultaneously at an overlapping position in any other inertial frame. We will now use these assumptions, along with the concept of a light clock, to demonstrate length contraction.

2.3 Time Dilation

Time passes more slowly for things moving relative to you; this is called time dilation. To explain why it happens, we will use the simple concept of a light clock. It consists of light bouncing back and forth between two mirrors. It keeps time by measuring when light returns to the first mirror and counting each return as one tick of its clock, as shown in Figure (2.2).


The light in the clock takes a time Δt in the clock's rest frame to make the return journey. We can see from Figure (2.2.a) that in the rest frame, the distance the light travels to the mirror and back in this time is

(2.8)2dm=cΔt.

The distance the mirrors move during this return journey in the moving frame is

(2.9)uΔt′=−vΔt′,

where Δt′ is the time it took light to return within the moving frame, and u is the speed of the light clock, which is in the opposite direction of the movement of the primed frame relative to the rest frame, that is, u=−v.

The distance light travels in this time is

(2.10)cΔt′

This is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle formed by uΔt′=−vΔt′ and 2dm, so we have the square of the hypotenuse equal to the squared sum of the other two lengths

(2.11)c2Δt′2=v2Δt′2+c2Δt2

rearranging this to find the time it took in the primed frame relative to the rest frame, we get

(2.12)Δt′=γΔt

with

(2.13)γ=11−v2c2.

This factor, γ (gamma), is used throughout special relativity to simplify equations. We can see from the diagram and the equations that the time for the return journey is longer in the frame with the clock moving relative to the clock's rest frame,

(2.14)Δt′≥Δt

We take this outcome to mean that the time between two events at the same position in the moving frame is longer than in the rest frame of the clock, because light must travel a longer distance, but at the same speed. Hence, moving systems seem to have time flow more slowly. An example of this is that unstable particles that are moving faster have longer lifespans before they decay.

The earlier time dilation equation (2.12) describes a transformation between a generic unprimed and primed frame. In later chapters, however, we will be describing specifically the rest frame of a source/particle. We will denote the rest frame's coordinates and properties with a subscript zero, and use unmarked variables for the observer's frame. Consequently, the time transformation shifts from Δt→Δt′ to Δt0→Δt, where Δt0 explicitly defines the time interval in the rest frame. This gives the updated time dilation equation:

(2.15)Δt=γΔt0

2.4 Length Contraction

An object's size decreases in the direction of motion compared to when it is at rest; this is called length contraction. To explain why it happens, we will add a second perpendicular light path to the experimental setup from the previous section. So there is now light moving perpendicular as well as parallel the primed frame's movement, as shown in Figure (2.3)


If we have a system as described in Figure (2.3). Then, since the light returns simultaneously in the rest frame, it must also return simultaneously in the second frame. Multiple events that occur at a single point simultaneously in a frame, must then occur simultaneously at a single point in all other frames. This is to ensure the second postulate holds true. The time between the light being emitted and absorbed will be the dilated time that we worked out in the previous section. As the sideways light path in this setup and the light clock's setup from the previous section is the same, hence it takes the same amount of time. In the moving frame, to achieve this simultaneity in the return of the light to the bulb, the length of the full path of light from the central bulb to the front mirror and back (2ΔZ′=zf′+zb′) must be the same as the perpendicular path, due to the speed of light being the same for both paths. We can work out the length of the sideways paths from the time dilation section, cΔt′, and this is also the total length the other path needs to be. We will find that the paths can only have this length if the distance between the bulb and the front mirror is contracted in the direction of movement. Note that there can not be a contraction in the perpendicular direction to the movement due to the paradox explained in Figure (1.12).

In the moving frame, the pulse sent forward has a path length equal to the speed of light multiplied by the time along for the path. Which is also equal to the primed frame's distance between the bulb and mirror plus the distance the mirror has moved away from the point it was emitted in this time, that is

(2.16)zf′=cΔtf′=ΔZ′+uΔtf′

where u is the speed that the front mirror is moving away from the point it was emitted, Δtf′ is the time taken to get to the mirror, and ΔZ′ is the distance between the bulb and the mirror in front in the primed frame. After reaching the mirror, the light then must travel back to the bulb a distance

(2.17)zb′=cΔtb′=ΔZ′−uΔtb′.

Where Δtb′ is the time taken to return to the bulb from the front mirror, with the source moving towards the reflected light.

These give the two times as

(2.18)Δtf′=ΔZ′c−u

and

(2.19)Δtb′=ΔZ′c+u.

Adding both these times together gives the total dilated time of return as

(2.20)Δt′=ΔZ′(1c+u+1c−u)=ΔZ′c21−u2/c2=2γ2ΔZ′c

where we used u=−v and the γ factor to simplify the equation. Now, from this and using the time dilation equation (2.12), we have

(2.21)cΔt′=cγΔt=2γΔZ=2γ2ΔZ′

Finally, this leads to the length from the bulb to the front mirror in the primed frame to be

(2.22)ΔZ′=1γΔZ.

This equation shows that for a system moving relative to an observer, the distances for the system in the direction of movement are contracted compared to the rest frame of the object, that is

(2.23)ΔZ′≤ΔZ.

Objects and the distance between them are therefore shorter in a frame with them moving compared to in the rest frame of the objects.

With this knowledge and the last section, we can now derive the coordinate transform equations.

2.5 Position and Time Transformation

In the last two sections, we have looked at the dilation between two different times at the same location and the contraction between two different positions at the same time, when we switch between frames. Now we will use both of these concepts to see how the combination of time and position coordinates, known as an event, transforms when we switch frames. For the derivation of the coordinate transformation of an event between two inertial frames, we will start with the same diagram we had in classical relativity in Section (2.1) and apply what we have learned from the time dilation and length contraction sections to maintain consistency with the postulates of special relativity. Our knowledge from this will allow us to derive the coordinate transformation equations, known as the Lorentz transformation.

As shown in the diagram, we are in the initial frame with origin o― defined by coordinates (0,0,0) and the primed frame is moving in the z-direction at velocity v such that the position of the primed origin in the initial frame is

(2.24)oo′→=(0,0,vt)

at time t from when the origins overlapped. If there is an event described by

(2.25)e―=(x,y,z,t)

Then the displacement between the initial frame's origin and the event's position in the initial frame is

(2.26)r―=(x,y,z)

and the displacement between the primed frame's origin and the event's coordinates in the initial frame is

(2.27)o′e→=(x,y,z−vt)

In the primed frame, we will have the event described by the primed coordinates that we want to transform into, as

(2.28)e―′=(x′,y′,z′,t′)

with the displacement between the primed frame's origin and the event's position in the primed frame given as

(2.29)r―′=(x′,y′,z′)

These are just the event's position coordinates in the primed frame.

The primed frame's axis and coordinates are moving relative to the initial frame, so from the previous length contraction section, we would have the displacement between the primed axis origin and the event in the initial frame o′e→, length contracted, in the z-direction, compared to the primed position coordinates in the primed frame r―′, that is

(2.30)o′e→=(x,y,z−vt)=(x′,y′,z′γ)

The x and y-components are unaffected, with the paradox of if they were affected, explained in Figure (1.12). Rearranging for the z-component, we have

(2.31)(x′,y′,z′)=r―′=(x,y,γ(z−vt))

There is symmetry between the frames: if we were originally in the primed frame, the initial frame would instead be moving at -v in the z-direction relative to the primed frame. We could instead follow the above steps, starting with the negative of the original frame velocity and the primed coordinate, and find that the inverse transformation is the same, except it swaps each frame's coordinates in the transform and uses the negative of the previous frame velocity instead. That is

(2.32)(x,y,z)=r―=(x′,y′,γ(z′+vt′))

We can substitute both z-coordinate transforms into each other to find the time transform

(2.33)z=γ(γ(z−vt)+vt′)

and rearranging gives

(2.34)t′=γ((1γ2−1)zv+t)

with 1/γ2=1−v2/c2 leading to the primed frames time for the event given in initial frames coordinates as

(2.35)t′=γ(t−vzc2)

Again, if we want the inverse transform from the primed to the initial frame, we can swap the primed and initial frame coordinates and add a minus sign to the frame velocity.

(2.36)t=γ(t′+vz′c2)

We now have the full description of the transformation of the position and time of an event as

(2.37)x′=xy′=yz′=γ(z−vt)with the time since the overlap of the coordinate axes:t′=γ(t−vzc2)with γ=11−v2c2

These are the equations that define special relativity. They allow us to find an event's position relative to the axis of the frame that we want to switch into.

In the time transform equation the vzc2 term is the cause of the simultaneity of events at two different positions in one inertial frame no longer being simultaneous in another inertial frame. The γ factor determines the overall change in how fast time flows at a point relative to the initial frame. In the spatial coordinate transform equations, the vt factor is due to both axes' origins moving away from each other, and the γ factor is the cause of the change of lengths in the direction of the frame's movement.

We can see how points representing the coordinates in an initial frame look like in a primed frame of reference by looking at Figure (2.5).


This diagram shows stationary points representing coordinates in the initial frame. These points are transformed to their primed frame positions z′=γz and are now moving at speed −v. They are transformed to points that are more spread out in the primed frame. However, the times at which they are located at each of these points are different (they have desynchronized times). Therefore, to find these points, which represent the coordinates in the initial frame, now in the primed frame at the synchronized time t′=0, we must propagate the points to that time, which results in z′=zγ, as shown in figure (2.5.c).

This figure is to give you a little more intuition on how the coordinates and switching between frames work. We will later see a more natural interpretation of the coordinate transforms when we introduce the notion of retarded time in Chapter (4), which will give us another reason why the time transformation is the way it is.

2.5.1 Transforms with Small Primed Frame Velocity

If we have the primed frame velocity much smaller than the speed of light (v≪c), then we have v/c≈0 and therefore γ≈1. Hence, we get back the previous classical transform equations

(2.38)t′≈t
(2.39)z′≈z−vt

Which is the expected result, as it agrees with the everyday observations we are used to seeing at these speeds. That is, no noticeable difference in clock times or the lengths of moving objects. We can see in Figure (2.6) when the γ-factor's influence becomes significant.

As can be seen, it is not until the primed frame velocity is approximately a third of the speed of light that it significantly differs from 1. The speed of light is a speed unattainable to us; the only thing we can bring up close to this speed is particles, and nothing human made can even reach a 1000th the speed of light.

2.5.2 Space and Time Intervals

To get the velocity transform equations, we first need the equations for transforming the displacement between two positions and the interval between two times, then take the limit as the changes go to zero. That is, when we have infinitesimal changes of coordinates. If we want to know how the displacement between two coordinates (x1,y1,z1) and (x2,y2,z2) transforms, we can take the difference of the transforms of both the coordinates as follows

(2.40)x2′−x1′=x2−x1y2′−y1′=y2−y1z2′−z1′=γ(z2−vt2)−γ(z1−vt1)t2′−t1′=γ(t2−vc2z2)−γ(t1−vc2z1)

rearranging and replacing the difference of the first and second of each coordinate with Δr―=(Δx,Δy,Δz)=(x2−x1,y2−y1,z2−z1), giving the displacement transform as

(2.41)Δx′=ΔxΔy′=ΔyΔz′=γ(Δz−vΔt)Δt′=γ(Δt−vc2Δz)

This transform has the same structural form as the coordinate transform equations.

From these equations, we can also get the differential quantities when we take infinitesimal changes, which give the same form again, as

(2.42)dx′=dxdy′=dydz′=γ(dz−vdt)dt′=γ(dt−vc2dz)

So, when we make an infinitesimally small change in position and/or time within a frame, we know what the corresponding change is in a primed frame. We will use these equations to get the velocity transform equations. The velocity at any instance is the infinitesimal change in position per infinitesimal change in time. These will also be used later to find invariant quantities, quantities that remain the same in each frame. For example, the space-time interval and the energy-momentum relationship in Chapter (3).

2.6 Velocity

The velocity at any instant is the infinitesimal change in position divided by the infinitesimal change in time: u―=dr―dt. So using the infinitesimals from Equation (2.42), we get the velocity in each direction as

(2.43)ux′=dx′dt′=dxγ(dt−vdzc2)uy′=dy′dt′=dyγ(dt−vdzc2)uz′=dz′dt′=γ(dz−vdt)γ(dt−vdzc2)

Now, dividing the top and bottom of the fraction on the right-hand side by dt, we can give the equations in their vector form as

(2.44)u―′=1γ(1−vc2uz)(uxuyγ(uz−v))at position r―′ and time t′

This transform is used to find the velocity of anything in another frame at the corresponding primed position and time. We will put this equation to work in a later section, when we look at how the light emitted by a source has its velocity's direction changed (aberrated) when transforming between frames, and the effect this has on the light's intensity in all directions. Next, we will use this to get the acceleration transform.

Side Note:

For those who are interested, the generalized velocity transform (which we will not derive here) for a frame velocity in any direction, and not just the z-direction, is

(2.45)u―′=1γu―+[γ−1‖v―‖2(u―⋅v―)−γ]v―1−u―⋅v―c2

with v― being the frame's velocity in any generalized direction.

2.7 Acceleration

To find how the acceleration (known as the 3-acceleration) of a particle transforms for observers in two different frames, we take the differential of the velocity transform in equation (2.44) and use the differentiation rules for two generic functions f and g: d(gf)=fdg+gdf, and d[f(g(x))]=dg(x)∗df(g(x))

(2.46)du―′=1γ(1−vc2uz)(duxduyγduz)+γvc2duzγ2(1−vc2uz)2(uxuyγ(uz−v))=...=1γ(1−vc2uz)2(dux+vc2(uxduz−uzdux)duy+vc2(uyduz−uzduy)1γduz)

Now, divide by dt′ as we did for the velocity in the previous section, and we get the acceleration transform as

(2.47)a―′=1γ2(1−vc2uz)3(ax+vc2(uxaz−uzax)ay+vc2(uyaz−uzay)1γaz)at position r―′ and time t′

So if we know how a particle accelerates in one frame, we will know its corresponding acceleration in another frame at the corresponding primed time and position.

Side Note:

Again, for those who are interested, the generalized acceleration transform (which we will not derive here) for a frame velocity in any direction and not just the z-direction is

(2.48)a―′=1γ3(1−(u―⋅v―)c2)3[γ(1−(u―⋅v―)c2)a―+γ(a―⋅v―)c2u―+(1−γ)(a―⋅v―^)⋅v―^]

at position r―′ and time t′. This equation is referred to as the 3-acceleration transform in other sources.

Now, when it comes to force, it is a bit more confusing. In classical/Galilean physics force can be described as the rate of change of momentum, or equivalently, as mass multiplied by the acceleration. But in special relativity, we define force as the rate of change of momentum alone, since momentum has an additional factor due to relativistic effects compared to the classical version, as explained in the next chapter. This extra term leads to a different formula for the force compared to the mass times the acceleration above.

2.8 The Paradox of Faster than Light Signals

Here, we will look at sending signals faster than the speed of light and see that this leads to the paradox that the time of events can change the order in which they happen in different reference frames. The thought experiment that examines this is called the Tachyonic Antitelephone and is as follows.

Consider two particles at rest in an initial reference frame, an emitting particle and a receiving particle, with the emitting particle located at the origin, and the receiving particle located on the positive z-axis at zr.

At time 0, the emitting particle at the origin emits a signal at speed us, which is received by the receiving particle at position zr at time tr=zr/us in this rest frame of the particles.

Now, consider a primed frame moving at speed v relative to the first. To find the emission and received times in the primed frame, we use the time transformation from equations (2.37). Giving the emission time as t′=0 and the time it was received as

(2.49)tr′=γ(tr−vzrc2)=γ(1−vusc2)tr

since γ and tr are positive, we have that if vus>c2, which is possible if us>c, then the time signal was received in the primed frame can actually end up being negative (i.e., before time of emission), meaning that you could have the receiving particle receive the signal before the emitting particle has sent it.

This thought experiment, by itself, does not completely rule out speeds faster than the speed of light. The mathematics does allow for it, but the possibility of the order of a cause and effect being interchangeable would contradict our intuition, even if the math itself stays consistent in all reference frames.

From this, many conclude that it should be impossible to send a signal faster than the speed of light. On top of this, there is also a restriction on particles with mass that leads to another barrier to speeds faster than light, which we will see later in section (3.3.7), which discusses specifically why particles with mass can not reach the speed of light, due to them requiring infinite energy to get to that speed.

2.9 Summary

In this chapter, we derived the mathematics for transforming spatial and time coordinates in classical relativity, which later helped us understand the derivation of special relativity. We then introduced the assumptions, known as the postulates of special relativity, which we use to derive how time slows down due to time dilation and how the lengths of moving objects contract. This led to the introduction of γ, which is a factor used throughout relativity to simplify equations. We then had the tools to derive the transformation equations, which in turn allowed us to calculate the velocity and acceleration transforms. Later in Chapter (4), we will take a look at the delayed view of the world an observer sees, due to the delay in light from their surroundings, and this will help us understand why we need the time transformation to be the way it is.

So we have learned how to transform from one reference frame into another, in special relativity. The outline of steps to transform a system of particles and their properties such as position, time, velocity, and acceleration, is as follows. If you have a system of particles in an initial frame, and you want to transform their positions to a new frame, you need to first define where the origin of this initial axis is. You are free to choose where it is. The primed frame's axis will overlap with this initial frame's axis at your arbitrarily chosen starting time, that is, when you define the time as t=0 (the time of the overlap is also t′=0 in the primed frame). You can now transform the positions into the primed frame. These particles have their primed frame positions at the calculated primed frame times, defined in Equations (2.37). To transform the velocities and acceleration of these particles at their primed frame positions at the corresponding primed times in the primed frame, you can use equations (2.47) and (2.44).

And this is all the steps needed, but an easy mistake to make is to forget that t and t′ are the times from the overlap of the frame origins in their respective frames.

This chapter laid the foundations of special relativity, but there is still more to come.

< Previous Next >

Chapter 3. Quantities That All Inertial Frames Agree On

Some quantities do not change when we transform between inertial reference frames. These frame-independent quantities are referred to as Lorentz invariant quantities.

The simplest quantity that all inertial frames agree on is the speed at which light propagates. When switching from an initial frame to a primed frame, the speed of light does not change, c′=c. We can equivalently express this using the light's velocity vector as ‖c―′‖=‖c―‖.

In this chapter, we will see more invariant quantities related to the space-time coordinates (x,y,z,t) and use them to find invariant properties associated with velocity, which will lead to the more abstract conservation relations among momentum, energy, and mass. We will find a new quantity with the units of energy that has a term which approximates to the kinetic energy of a particle at low velocities and another term that suggests particles have another type of energy, which was not previously in classical physics, that depends on the mass of a particle (mass-energy equivalence). This new quantity will lead to a new conservation law of energy. The reason we care about the concept of energy is that it has a conservation law, which we will learn about later, that can be used as a tool to help us make calculations and model more complex systems.

3.1 The Space-Time Interval

An event in special relativity is defined by its position and time coordinates x, y, z, and t. These are called its space-time coordinates. The changes in the coordinates between two events are denoted as Δx, Δy, Δz, and Δt.

From these, we could define a quantity called the space-time interval ΔS between two events in an inertial reference frame as:

(3.1)ΔS2=(cΔt)2−Δx2−Δy2−Δz2

The reason we care about this new quantity is that all inertial frames of reference agree on the space-time interval between two events; it is invariant between frames, ΔS=ΔS′. The invariance can be shown to be true when we substitute the coordinate transforms from equation (2.41) into the primed version of this last equation:

(3.2)ΔS′2=(cΔt′)2−Δx′2−Δy′2−Δz′2=c2γ(Δt−vc2Δz)2−Δx2−Δy2−Δ(γ(Δz−vΔt))2=(cΔt)2−Δx2−Δy2−Δz2=ΔS2.

This relationship will come in very useful in the later energy, mass, and momentum sections.

3.2 D'Alembert operator

(This can be seen as a bonus section that may be skipped, as it is not directly relevant to the understanding of any other sections in this text.)

The d'Alembert operator is fundamental in relativistic wave equations; it is invariant in all frames of reference. It is denoted as ◻, and consists of the second-order partial derivatives with respect to each coordinate. It is defined in an initial frame as

(3.3)◻=1c2∂2∂t2−(∂2∂x2+∂2∂y2+∂2∂z2)

and in a primed frame as

(3.4)◻′=1c2∂2∂t′2−∂2∂x′2−∂2∂y′2−∂2∂z′2

In the following derivation, we will show that it is invariant; this will be done by transforming the partial derivatives between reference frames and showing that the operator retains its form, and that ◻′=◻.

From the transformation equations (2.37), we can get all partial derivatives, which we will use to transform the equations between frames:

(3.5)∂x′∂x=1∂y′∂x=0∂z′∂x=0∂t′∂x=0∂x′∂y=0∂y′∂y=1∂z′∂y=0∂t′∂y=0∂x′∂z=0∂y′∂z=0∂z′∂z=γ∂t′∂z=−γvc2∂x′∂t=0∂y′∂t=0∂z′∂t=−γv∂t′∂t=γ

To find the partial derivatives with respect to the unprimed coordinates, in terms of the partial derivatives with respect to the primed coordinates, we can use the chain rule. Which for ∂∂t is:

(3.6)∂∂t=∂t′∂t∂∂t′+∂x′∂t∂∂x′+∂y′∂t∂∂y′+∂z′∂t∂∂z′

and for ∂∂z:

(3.7)∂∂z=∂t′∂z∂∂t′+∂x′∂z∂∂x′+∂y′∂z∂∂y′+∂z′∂z∂∂z′

Substituting the partial derivatives from above into these chain rule expressions, yields:

(3.8)∂∂x=∂∂x′∂∂y=∂∂y′∂∂z=−γvc2∂∂t′+γ∂∂z′∂∂t=γ∂∂t′−γv∂∂z′

Now, we can get the second-order partial derivatives, which are the same as applying the first-order partial derivative twice, which gives

(3.9)∂2∂t2=∂∂t⋅∂∂t=(γ∂∂t′−γv∂∂z′)(γ∂∂t′−γv∂∂z′)=γ2∂2∂t′2−2γ2v∂2∂t′∂z′+γ2v2∂2∂z′2
(3.10)∂2∂z2=(−γvc2∂∂t′+γ∂∂z′)(−γvc2∂∂t′+γ∂∂z′)=γ2v2c4∂2∂t′2−2γ2vc2∂2∂t′∂z′+γ2∂2∂z′2
(3.11)∂2∂x2=∂2∂x′2∂2∂y2=∂2∂y′2

We can now substitute these transformed second derivatives into equation (3.3) to get the d'Alembert operator.

Let us first do this for just the t and z components (1c2∂2∂t2−∂2∂z2):

(3.12)1c2∂2∂t2−∂2∂z2=1c2(γ2∂2∂t′2−2γ2v∂2∂t′∂z′+γ2v2∂2∂z′2)−(γ2v2c4∂2∂t′2−2γ2vc2∂2∂t′∂z′+γ2∂2∂z′2)=1c2(γ2∂2∂t′2+γ2v2∂2∂z′2)−(γ2v2c4∂2∂t′2+γ2∂2∂z′2)=1c2∂2∂t′2−∂2∂z′2

Now adding in the x and y components, to get the full d'Alembert operator in both frames:

(3.13)1c2∂2∂t2−∂2∂x2−∂2∂y2−∂2∂z2=1c2∂2∂t′2−∂2∂x′2−∂2∂y′2−∂2∂z′2

As can be seen in this equation, the left-hand side is the D'Alembert operator in the initial frame's coordinates, and the right-hand side is the D'Alembert operator in the primed frame's coordinates.

So we can conclude that the D'Alembert operator in both frames are equal:

(3.14)◻′=◻

Thus, we have demonstrated that the d'Alembert operator maintains its form under an inertial frame transformation, confirming its invariance. The invariance of this is a direct consequence of the way transformations preserve the spacetime interval.

3.3 Energy-Mass and Momentum Relation

When it comes to the relationships among energy, mass, and momentum, there are many different derivations. But there is no straightforward derivation that avoids all downsides, such as hidden assumptions. I wanted to avoid a derivation that seems good on the surface but has its flaws hidden, or just ignored. So I decided to at least start with a strong foundation, and point out any assumptions as we derive it. To do this, we will start with a quantity that we know is invariant, and from it get a quantity with the units of energy that is invariant, which we will use to derive the full relationship. We will use some mathematical tricks, such as the Taylor expansion, and make reasonable interpretations of each term in the equation. For instance, there are quantities in the equations we will encounter later that we will interpret as the total energy and the inherent energy a particle at rest has due to its mass. These interpretations do indeed turn out to agree with experiments [3, 4], which is what matters.

So let us begin by deriving the invariant energy quantity.

3.3.1 The Invariant Energy Quantity

Here, we derive the invariant energy quantity of a particle from the spacetime interval.

We can see from equation (3.1) that if a particle q is moving in an inertial reference frame, we can define the space-time interval of its coordinates in this frame as

(3.15)ΔSq2=c2Δtq2−Δxq2−Δyq2−Δzq2

We will not change reference frames anywhere in these next sections. And since we will remain in the same reference frame, we will not need to make use of any primed notation (′) here.

Now we can divide this space-time interval by the square of the proper time that passes for the particle in this interval Δt0 (the interval in time that passes in the particle's rest frame). The proper time is the time that all frames of reference agree on and that keeps the expression invariant. Now, taking the limit as the change in proper time in the interval goes to zero, we get a derivative that is an abstract invariant quantity that we will call the space-time velocity:

(3.16)(dSqdt0)2=(cdtqdt0)2−(dxqdt0)2−(dyqdt0)2−(dzqdt0)2

From the time dilation equation (2.15) (using Δt0=dt0 and Δt=dtq), we have dt0=dtq/γu with γu=11−uq2c2. This allows us to reduce this space-time velocity to the following:

(3.17)(dSqdt0)2=γu2(cdtqdtq)2−γu2(dxqdtq)2−γu2(dyqdtq)2−γu2(dzqdtq)2=c2γu2(1−uqx2+uqy2+uqz2c2)=c2γu2(1−uq2c2)=c2

It can be seen that this space-time velocity is still an invariant quantity as the speed of light is constant in all frames.

Now we could multiply both sides of the third line in equation (3.17) by the invariant quantity m2c2, where m is the invariant rest mass of the particle, so that we get

(3.18)m2c2(dSqdt0)2=m2c4γu2(1−uq2c2)(mc2)2=γu2m2c4−γu2m2uq2c2

where (dSqdt0)2=c2 was substituted in, to get the final equation.

This final equation's terms are all in units of energy squared, with the invariant energy squared term on the left, which we will tidy up so that we can write it as

(3.19)(mc2)2=(γumc2)2−(γumuqc)2

This invariant expression will serve as our basis for deriving everything in the following sections.

3.3.2 Rest Mass-Energy Equivalence

Equation (3.19) shows an invariant quantity with the units of energy squared (mc2)2; from this, we have the energy term mc2 itself being invariant; it is an energy that is the same in all frames of reference.

If we interpret this not just as mathematical but also as having physical meaning, then this would be a new type of energy associated with every particle, previously unknown before special relativity. This energy does not depend on the speed of a particle; it is an intrinsic energy all masses have, even when at rest. We call this the rest mass energy, written as

(3.20)E0=mc2

From this, we can deduce that if the mass of a system of particles decreases, then the decrease in energy due to the loss of mass must be offset by an increase in other forms of energy to keep the system's energy conserved. For example, this can be done by converting the energy previously stored in its mass into energy in the form of light. This conversion of energy is consistent with experimental results.

Although this equivalence has been misused to make nuclear bombs, you can thank it for the ability to generate energy from decaying radioactive elements in nuclear power plants and for the future possibility of generating energy from nuclear fusion plants. It also helps explain why stars can produce so much energy, as they convert some of their mass into energy in the form of light, through nuclear fusion reactions.

Now, looking at the rest mass energy equation, it does not seem like a very proper way to derive this famous equation, or at least it looks like we have taken a shortcut. But let us continue, and we will look at what the other terms in equation (3.19) represent, to see if we get anything else that may convince us a little more that this is an okay interpretation of this invariant quantity of energy.

To do this, we will first derive the relativistic version of momentum.

3.3.3 Relativistic Momentum

We will now look at the other two terms in equation (3.19); both contain the gamma function, and we will use the Taylor series approximation to obtain more information about each term.

So let us rearrange equation (3.19), to get

(3.21)(γumc2)2=(mc2)2+(γumuqc)2

for the energy term in the brackets on the left-hand side, we can use what is called the Taylor expansion to write γu as a convergent series:

(3.22)γu≡1+12uq2c2+38uq4c4+...

Giving the energy term on the left-hand side as

(3.23)γumc2=mc2(1+12uq2c2+38uq4c4+...)=mc2+12muq2+38muq4c2+...

The first quantity in this equation is an energy that does not depend on the particle's speed. It is the invariant energy from before, the rest mass energy. The second quantity is the classical kinetic energy formula. The rest may be viewed as higher-order kinetic energy terms, which are absent in classical physics because they are very small for uq≪c. So this seems like it could be a formula for the particle's total energy (in a vacuum, with no potential energy). We will denote this total energy as

(3.24)E=γumc2

and the rest mass energy from the last section, denoted as E0, allowing us to write equation (3.21) as

(3.25)E2=E02+(γumuqc)2

Now, let us look at this last energy term in the brackets, along with the Taylor expansion of γu, giving

(3.26)γucmuq=cmuq(1+12uq2c2+38uq4c4+...)=c(muq+12muq3c2+38muq5c4+...)

At small particle velocities, this last term is approximately (muq)c with muq being the classical momentum; it seems like this energy could be the relativistic version of the particle's momentum, times the speed of light.

So we will think of the last term in equation (3.25) as the relativistic momentum of the particle:

(3.27)p=γumuq

which is approximately the classical momentum at speeds much less than the speed of light.

3.3.4 Proof that the relativistic Momentum is Conserved

Classically, we have conservation laws for momentum and energy, meaning that for an isolated system, both remain constant. For an isolated system of particles, the total energy and the momentum of all the particles before an interaction is the same as the total energy and the momentum of all the particles after,

(3.28)pafter=pbeforeEafter=Ebefore

In classical physics, we only cared about these two quantities because they have these conservation laws; if they did not, they would not be useful.

Hence, we would like for there to still be conservation laws in special relativity for the relativistic versions of the quantities. And for these conservation laws to hold, we would need them to hold in all inertial frames of reference.

So we will show that if the total energy and relativistic momentum are conserved in one frame, then they are conserved in all reference frames.
