We will start with the previous definitions of momentum and total energy: p―=γumu― and E=γumc2.

Transformation Identities

We choose the primed frame to move in the z-direction as usual, giving the velocity transform between the frames from equation (2.44). We will also make use of an identity for γu′ given by

(3.29)γu′=γuγ(1−uzvc2)

I will let you check this identity yourself, as it is just the substitution of the transform equation of u′ into the gamma function, with some rearrangement.

Y-Component

Using equation (2.44) and equation (3.29) on the relativistic momentum's y-component in the primed frame py′=γu′muy′, gives:

(3.30)py′=[γuγ(1−uzvc2)]m[uyγ(1−uzvc2)]py′=γumuypy′=py

In the y-direction, the equation for the momentum is unchanged. Therefore, if the momentum is conserved before and after an event in the initial frame, it is still conserved in the primed frame. This new relativistic momentum is required to allow for the conservation law to work between different frames for the y-component.

Z-Component

Now doing the same for the z-component pz′=γu′muz′, we get:

(3.31)pz′=[γuγ(1−uzvc2)]m[uz−v1−uzvc2]pz′=γuγm(uz−v)pz′=γ(γumuz)−γv(γum)
Proof of Conservation

Using the relativistic momentum in the initial frame pz=γumuz and the equation for the total energy that we described in the previous section E=γumc2, we obtain:

(3.32)pz′=γ(pz−vEc2)

now, if we do have the total momentum and total energy before and after conserved, we have

(3.33)Δpz′=γ(pzafter−vEafterc2)−γ(pzbefore−vEbeforec2)=γ(Δpz−vΔEc2)

This last equation is the transformation of the momentum in the z-direction of each particle to a primed frame.

In the isolated system in the initial frame, we want both the momentum and energy to be conserved

(3.34)Δpz=0ΔE=0

If these are indeed conserved, then

(3.35)Δpz′=0

giving the momentum conserved in the z-direction in the primed frame as well.

So the momentum is conserved in all the components in the primed frame. Therefore, taking the γumuq term as being the relativistic momentum and the term γumc2 as the total energy is consistent with special relativity and the laws of the conservation of momentum and energy.

Now, what about for light itself, when γ is infinitely large, can we still get the energy-momentum relation to work?

3.3.5 Momentum of Light

Here, we will show how to get the only reasonable momentum equation of light that we can from the energy-momentum relationship equation.

So let us start by rewriting the energy-momentum equation (3.25).

(3.36)E2=(mc2)2+(γumuqc)2

For the speed of light, we have γu being infinitely large, so if the photon had a non-zero rest mass, the second term would be infinite, therefore giving the total energy as infinite, which is not possible. So the photon must have zero (or at least only infinitesimal) rest mass, giving zero for the first term (rest mass energy), reducing the total energy of a photon to;

(3.37)Eph=(γcmphc)c

now, if we were to get a finite energy from this, we would require γcmph (which is an infinite value multiplied by an infinitesimal) to be finite for it to give a meaningful energy of the photon. We previously used the term p=γum to represent the relativistic momentum of a particle. So we could take this term as representing the photon's momentum as well, and think of meff=γcmph as the "effective mass" that a photon has, giving its momentum as pph=meffc. Therefore, the momentum for light in terms of its energy as

(3.38)pph=Ephc

with pph and Eph being the momentum and energy of the photon.

This equation for the energy-momentum relationship of light can also be derived in electromagnetic theory [5], which gives us more confidence that we are correct.

The last equation allows us to generalize the last energy term in equation (3.25), as the momentum times the speed of light

(3.39)Ep=pc

giving us the final piece of the puzzle.

3.3.6 Energy-Mass-Momentum Relation

Now that we have confirmed the use of relativistic momentum from equation (3.27), we can substitute it and equation (3.20) into (3.25) to finally obtain the famous energy-momentum relationship:

(3.40)E2=(mc2)2+(pc)2

with momentum being p=γumuq for a particle with mass, and written more meaningfully for a photon as p=E/c.

Side Note:

When looking at particle collisions, we also need to take into account potential energy as particles move towards and away from each other, but this must take into account for acceleration as well. which is not an easy thing to do.

3.3.7 Speed of Light Limit

Previously, we showed that faster than light travel would lead to effects being able to occur before their cause, in section (2.8), but here is another reason why faster than light transport may not be possible for particles with mass.

We can see from the total energy equation (3.24), that if a particle with mass were accelerated to the speed of light, its energy would become infinite. So we would need infinite energy (which does not exist) to get that particle to the speed of light. Therefore, it is not possible.

If you still want to consider the possibility of a particle moving at speeds faster than light speed, it would lead to γ being imaginary (the square root of a negative number). But we require that energy be a real quantity for it to be measurable, and for this, we would need the mass to be imaginary as well. Some Physicists theorized a particle with an imaginary mass, the tachyon, but this still has the problem that cause and effect are interchangeable, as we explained in section (2.8). The tachyon has never been detected in any detectors.

3.4 Summary

In this chapter, we looked at the space-time interval, which is a very important quantity in special relativity. It is the simplest quantity that is invariant when switching between inertial reference frames (It has the same value in all inertial frames of reference). From this, we derived the D'Alembert operator, an important operator in relativistic wave equations. We showed that it is also invariant when switching between inertial reference frames.

The space-time interval also allowed us to find an invariant quantity with the units of energy. This led us to the concepts of a particle's rest mass energy, the total relativistic energy, and relativistic momentum. From this, we showed that these were consistent with the conservation laws for energy and momentum; if they were true in one inertial frame, they then hold in all inertial frames. Next, we found the relation between energy and momentum for light. which finally enabled us to write the energy-momentum equation in a more meaningful way.

In this chapter, we learned that mass and energy are equivalent, that particles with mass would require infinite energy to be accelerated to the speed of light, and that our definition of momentum needed to be updated to apply to light as well.

What we have learned here brings us to the boundary between pure special relativity and particle physics, which relies heavily on experimental physics to discover the rules that particles follow. Interactions between particles that produce other particles, require more than just conservation of energy and momentum to fully describe them; there is also the conservation of charge, lepton number, baryon number, etc., which determine which interactions can and can not happen. Hence, this is outside the context of this book.

So we will move on to Part (3), where we will take a close look at how light's propagation behaves in special relativity. We will first examine the delayed view of the world an observer sees due to the delay in light signals from their surroundings, and then move on to how light is affected when emitted from a moving point source, leading to many insights, including the famous Doppler effect.

< Previous Next >

Part III.
Light in Special Relativity

Here, we will discuss the propagation of light and its properties. We will look at the delay in light's signal due to the finite speed of light, and the effects of the principles of special relativity on the emission of light from a moving source. A lot of the concepts in the Chapters of this Part are not taught in most resources that you will find on special relativity, even though they can be very insightful. The exception to this is the Doppler effect on light's frequency, which is discussed in most resources and is derived here.

Chapter 4. An Observer's Delayed Worldview

Light travels extremely fast compared to other everyday speeds we are used to, roughly at 300,000,000 meters per second. In the blink of an eye, light could travel around the world twice. So we do not normally need to worry about delays in the light signal, as the time for light to propagate over the distances in our everyday world is extremely short. Therefore, the signal can be approximated as being instantaneous, and we can ignore the more complex modeling of the delayed light signal. But when it comes to particle physics or astronomy, we might be dealing with speeds close to that of light or huge distances. For example, light has taken 152,000 years to travel from the Andromeda Galaxy, so we are currently seeing the Andromeda Galaxy where it was and how it looked 152,000 years ago. Their past positions, which we currently see them in, are called their retarded positions. The topic in this chapter is not normally included in Special relativity texts. Still, it is necessary to give you a fuller story and better understanding of relativity. These topics provide additional insights into why the coordinate transform equations have to be the way they are. As we will see when transforming retarded positions between frames.

4.1 Retarded Coordinates

In an initial frame, we have its own coordinates at rest. If a light signal is emitted from a coordinate to an observer at the origin, it takes time to reach the observer, so the observer would see the stationary coordinate at the previous time that the light was emitted from this coordinate. This previous time is the position coordinate's retarded time.


As shown in the diagram, if we take the rest frame of an observer and a source that emits a pulse of light from its position at r―=r―ret so that it is received by the observer at the origin, at time t=0. The retarded time the pulse of light was emitted is

(4.1)tret=−‖r―ret‖c,

which is the negative of the time it took for light to propagate along r―ret to the origin. The velocity of the light that propagated to the origin is

(4.2)c―=c(0sin⁡αcos⁡α)

Where α is the direction of propagation. This velocity and the retarded time (which is negative) give the retarded position at which the light was emitted:

(4.3)r―ret=−‖r―ret‖c^―=ctret(0sin⁡αcos⁡α)

The source's current position and its retarded position are the same in its rest frame, since the source is not moving. Also, the position vector and the light's velocity vector are in opposite directions. A negative emission time reverses the direction of the velocity vector here. Now, inputting this retarded position and time into the coordinate transform, we get the retarded position and time in the primed frame as

(4.4)r―ret′=ctret(0sin⁡αγ(cos⁡α−vc))=(0yγ(z−vtret))at retarded time tret′=γ(1−vccos⁡α)tret

If instead we use the angle of the retarded coordinate from the z-axis, θret=α−π, we have that cos⁡α=cos⁡(θret+π)=−cos⁡θret and therefore the retarded time can be given as

(4.5)tret′=γ(1+vccos⁡θret)tret

With the light being received at the origin of the primed frame axis at time t′=0.

The coordinate transform here for retarded coordinates is the normal coordinate transform, except the time transform simplifies and allows us to take the retarded time out of brackets with just the factor ÅÅ=γ(1−vccos⁡α)=γ(1+vccos⁡θret) now in front of it. This factor will also come up in the Doppler effect, in aberration, and when finding the density of light from a source that is emitting it continuously in all directions. We can use this factor to simplify equations as we did with γ previously. We will call ÅÅ the aberrational factor, also known as the relativistic Doppler factor.

When switching to the primed frame, the angles at which light is emitted and received change; this is called the relativistic aberration of light. This aberration will be described fully in the next chapter.

Side Note:

This retarded position of the source is at its retarded time. If you wanted to find the position of the source at the same time as the observer, t′=0, we need to propagate it from its retarded position and time to this time of zero. So we need to take into account that the source is moving at u=−v and the retarded time is the negative of the time that we want to pass, for the source to move to its current position. These negatives cancel out. Which gives the current position, with a bit of working out, as

(4.6)r―t′=0′=r―ret′+v―tret′=ctret(0sin⁡α1γcos⁡α)

So for a stationary source in the rest frame at t=0, we have this position in the primed frame at t′=0.

4.2 The Transformed Retarded Coordinates

If we treat the coordinates of a coordinate system as retarded sources of light in the same way as we did for the source in the previous section, we can transform these retarded coordinates of the initial frame into the primed frame. This transform is shown in the figure below for a small subset of coordinates, to give you an idea of how the initial frame's retarded coordinates are spread in the primed frame.


The density of the initial frame's retarded coordinates in its own frame is constant everywhere, but in the primed frame, the initial frame's coordinates have a density that depends on the angle, as shown in the figure below. This figure is shown but not derived, as this requires mathematics from later in section (6.2).

If we are at rest in the initial frame, and we see the points as they are shown in the initial frame in figure (4.2.a), then if there were another observer overlapping with us moving at v―, they would see all the points distributed as they are shown in their primed frame in figure (4.2.b).

4.3 Apparent Velocity

From the previous section, we saw that objects appear to be at their retarded positions due to the delay in the light signal from them. That would also mean that we have the rate of change of the observed positions differing from their actual rate of change. That is, the apparent velocity of an object is different from its actual velocity. This concept of apparent velocity was demonstrated in section (1.13), where we saw that objects can be perceived as moving faster than light even if they are not actually doing so. Here, we will show how to find the Apparent velocity of objects.

If we have a moving particle at its retarded position r―ret, then in an infinitesimal time dt it will move by a displacement of u―retdt to position r―ret+u―retdt, as shown in the Diagram below (where u―ret is the velocity of the particle at the retarded time).

The difference between the retarded times of light from each position reaching the origin is the time that light takes to get from position r―ret+u―retdt minus the time it takes to get from position r―ret, plus the time it takes for the particle to move to the new position, dt. Which is

(4.7)dtret=‖r―+u―retdt‖c−‖r―‖c+dt

Since u―retdt is infinitesimally small, we can simplify this expression by using some approximations as shown in the following derivation.

(4.8)‖r―ret+u―retdt‖=(r―ret+u―retdt)⋅(r―ret+u―retdt)=r―ret⋅r―ret+2r―ret⋅u―retdt+u―ret2dt2≈r―ret⋅r―ret+2r―ret⋅u―retdt≈‖r―ret‖1+2r―ret⋅u―retdtr―ret⋅r―retusing the Taylor expansion 1+N≈1+N2for N≪1:≈‖r―ret‖(1+r―ret⋅u―retdt‖r―ret‖2)≈‖r―ret‖+r―ret⋅u―retdt‖r―ret‖≈‖r―ret‖+r^ret―⋅u―retdt

So, for the infinitesimal change in retarded positions we have ‖r―ret+u―retdt‖=‖r―ret‖+r^ret―⋅u―retdt, which we can substitute into equation (4.7) to get the time that has passed between the two positions as observed from the origin i.e., the perceived retarded time that has passed at the origin, given as

(4.9)dtret=dt+r^ret―⋅u―retdtc=dt+r^ret―⋅u―retdtc=(1+u―ret⋅r^ret―c)dt

The distances between the points are the same for the observer as the true distances between them; it is just the perceived retarded times that differ. Therefore, we can get this apparent velocity as

(4.10)u―app=u―retdtdtret=u―retdt(1+u―ret⋅r^ret―c)dt=u―ret1+u―ret⋅r^ret―c

This equation shows that the apparent velocity can be much larger or smaller, depending on the direction of motion of the object. For something moving at the speed of light, we have the apparent velocity being between 0.5c≤‖u―app‖≤∞ depending on the direction it is moving.

This section highlights an important concept that needs to be taken into account when making some experimental observations, such as the motion of stars, planets, and galaxies in astrophysics.

4.4 Summary

In this chapter, we introduced retarded positions, which are the positions an observer perceives objects to currently be at due to the delay in the light signal from the object to the observer, with their associated retarded time, which is the negative of the propagation time light takes to travel from the retarded position to the observer. We also derived how to transform these retarded coordinates to the corresponding prime frame's retarded coordinates. The retarded coordinate transform and also the density of the transformed initial frame's retarded coordinates in the primed frame were shown in figure (4.2) and figure (4.3) respectively. We then derived the apparent velocity of objects, which is the velocity an observer perceives an object to be moving at, which is consequence of the delay in the light signal. This velocity differs from the object's actual speed.

What we have learned in this chapter will be used later when performing transformations on light pulses.

Chapter 5. A Point Source: Emitting a Pulse of Light

If a light pulse is emitted from a point source in all directions in its rest frame, how will this be affected in a frame where the source is now moving? Answering this question will be the topic of this chapter. For this, we will look at the velocity transform specifically for the speed of light, which will be used throughout this chapter, then move on to look at the effect the transform has on the frequency of light that a source emits, the "Doppler effect". Next, we will get to "relativistic aberration", which explains how the angle at which the emitted light is propagated is affected. The combined effects of these together is called "relativistic beaming". Knowing all this will allow us to transform a field of continuously emitted light from a source in the next chapter and determine its properties. But to allow us to do all this, we will first need to describe the mathematics of spherical polar coordinates. The topics of relativistic aberration and beaming in this chapter are not covered in most special relativity sources. But they are interesting and offer important insights. So, They can be worth your while to learn.

5.1 Spherical Polar Coordinates

Before we go any further with special relativity, we will need to take some time making sure we know the math needed for what comes next. This section will be about spherical polar coordinates, which will help us describe how the propagation of light changes between frames, by allowing us to explain aberration, which is how the propagation angle changes between frames, and the Doppler effect, which is how the wavelength of light changes between frames. So let us start with how to describe a vector in terms of the spherical polar coordinates, which is shown in the following figure in red:

The figure shows that, for a given position r―, we can write it in Cartesian coordinates as (x,y,z), or in spherical polar coordinates as (r,θ,ϕ). Where the angles from the Z-Axis and X-axis are θ (between 0 and π) and ϕ (between 0 and 2π) respectively, and r is the displacement to the position from the origin.

The position can be written using either coordinate system as follows

(5.1)r―=(xyz)=r(cos⁡ϕsin⁡θsin⁡ϕsin⁡θcos⁡θ)

with

(5.2)r=‖r―‖=x2+y2+z2cos⁡θ=zrcos⁡ϕ=xx2+y2

This is all we shall need to know about spherical polar coordinates for this chapter. We will need to derive some more math beyond this in the next chapter, but we will look at it when it comes up.

5.2 Velocity Transform of Light from a Source

From here, we will explicitly use the source's rest frame and the frame in which the source is moving at speed u. We will denote the terms in the rest frame with a subscript zero (i.e., term0), and the moving frame with unaltered notation, as it will be the moving frame that we will be interested in finding information about, and it will allow to read equations for this chapter and the next more easily. Think of it as the frame with the moving source being the current frame and the rest frame being the one we need to compare to. Now, let us get back to it.

The speed of light remains the same after transforming between frames, but the velocity does not, because the direction of propagation changes. Light emitted at a speed c from a source at rest, at an angle α0 from the z-axis and φ0 from the x-axis, has the velocity written in spherical polar coordinates as

(5.3)c―0=c⋅c^―0=c(cos⁡φ0sin⁡α0sin⁡φ0sin⁡α0cos⁡α0),

Then, for the frame in which the source moves at speed u in the z-direction, we have this frame moving at v=−u relative to the rest frame. So, using the velocity transform from equation (2.44), we get the light's velocity in this frame as

(5.4)c―=c(cos⁡φsin⁡αsin⁡φsin⁡αcos⁡α)=cγ(1+uccos⁡α0)(cos⁡φ0sin⁡α0sin⁡φ0sin⁡α0γ(cos⁡α0+uc))

Using a bit of trigonometry to find the z-components in terms of sines instead of cosines, and substituting them into the other two components, you can find that φ=φ0.

This frame's velocity still has the speed of light, which can be seen by taking the magnitude of the velocity vector. However, the angle of propagation from the z-axis has changed; the change in this angle is described from the z-components of the equation above, as

(5.5)cos⁡α=(cos⁡α0+uc)(1+uccos⁡α0)

This is the relativistic aberration formula [6], which shows how the direction of light's propagation transforms, as shown in Figure (5.2). Rearranging this equation gives us the coordinate conversion in the opposite direction.

(5.6)cos⁡α0=(cos⁡α−uc)(1−uccos⁡α)

These equations, which show how the cosine of the propagation angle of the emitted light changes, will be put to use in the next section.

5.3 Aberration in Special Relativity

We have just derived how the propagation angle of light changes when switching frames. Here, we shall visually demonstrate the changes in propagation angle by looking at the following situation.

If a source in its rest frame emits light evenly in all directions, then each emitted light's angle of propagation is transformed using equation (5.4). The angles between the light's propagation and the z-axis, in the source's moving frame, are found using equation (5.5). This is shown in the following diagram.


The diagram shows that the moving source emits more radiation in the direction of its motion, compared to its rest frame. This is called relativistic aberration. If we want to see the opposite, with light instead being absorbed instead of emitted, we can look at the following figure.


For the case of a source, as its speed tends to the speed of light, u/c tends to 1, and from equation (5.5), we can see that, as a result of this, cos⁡α tends to 1. This means that all emitted light from the source tends to the direction of its motion as its speed tends to c. We also have that the flow of time for a moving source relative to its rest frame will become infinitely slow, coming to a stop, when moving at the speed of light. That is, the act of emitting the light stalls. For both these reasons, the light would remain in the vicinity of the source. I will leave this for you to contemplate.

5.4 Doppler Effect

When we switch between frames, the wavelength of light changes. This is called the Doppler effect and was shown by the color shift in the figures from the previous section. We will describe this effect using the help of the following simple figure of light being emitted from a source in its rest frame and in a frame in which it is moving.


In the rest frame of the source, if it emits a wave at the speed of light in any direction, we have the length the wave has traveled from the source in the infinitesimal time dt0 as being

(5.7)dλ0=cdt0

If we change to a frame where the source is moving at velocity u― in the z-direction, the wave is emitted at an angle α from the z-axis. It travels a distance cdt in a time dt, with the source moving a distance udtcos⁡α in the direction of the emitted wave. It leads to a bunching up of the wave in the direction of the movement of the source, as the same amount of the wave has been emitted in this frame's corresponding time, but the distance it has traveled from the source is

(5.8)dλ=cdt−ucos⁡αdt=(1−uccos⁡α)cdt=γ(1−uccos⁡α)cdt0

With dt=γdt0 being used in the last step, from the time dilation equation (2.15) (using Δt0=dt0 and Δt=dt substituted in. The ratio of the displacement of the wave compared to its displacement in the rest frame is

(5.9)dλdλ0=γ(1−uccos⁡α)

Wavelength is inversely proportional to the frequency, and this bunching up at the front will proportionally decrease the wavelength. The frequency ratio ν/ν0 is then

(5.10)νν0=dλ0dλ=1γ(1−uccos⁡α)

This gives us the formula for the frequency of light emitted by a moving source relative to its frequency in the source's rest frame.

This frequency shift can be used in astronomy to determine how fast stars and galaxies are moving relative to Earth. It is done by measuring the frequency of light from the star/galaxy and comparing it to the expected frequency if it were at rest, with the expected frequency calculated using some astrophysics, which we won't go into here. But for those who are interested, there are two videos explaining how we work such things out in astrophysics (part 1, part 2).

5.4.1 Frequency Change from switching Frame

The previous section shows how to calculate the frequency of light in a source's moving frame relative to its rest frame. But, if you want the frequency change of light, when you switch from any initial frame to a primed frame, then you can get it in terms of the primed frame's velocity v as

(5.11)ν′ν=γ(1−vccos⁡α)=1γ(1+vccos⁡α′)

5.5 Relativistic Beaming

Relativistic beaming is the combination of both effects from the two previous sections. To show it, we will look at a light pulse emitted from a source in its rest frame and how it appears in a frame where the source is moving. First, by applying the Lorentz transform to the pulse and source, and then propagating the pulse backwards or forwards in time to sync the light's times with the source at the origin.


The pulse's positions in the moving frame, with pulse's times synced with the source at the origin are shown in figure (5.5.c). They can be found from the Lorentz transformed rest frame's coordinates shown in figure (5.5.b) by propagating the light forward or backwards in time from these transformed coordinates to be synced with the origin's time of zero. So the light's position in the moving frame at the time of zero is

(5.12)l―=r―−c―t

Where r― is the light's positions from the Lorentz transformed rest frame coordinates at the Lorentz transformed time t, with c― being the velocity of light in the moving frame.

What we have learned here can be extended to multiple pulses, which we will do in the next chapter to see what a field of light pulses from a moving source would look like.

5.6 Retarded Propagation of Light in a Source's Moving Frame

There is a delay between when the light is emitted from a source and when it reaches a receiver; this is the propagation time Tp. As a result, there is a difference between where you are seeing moving objects and where they are currently. If the object is moving at velocity u―, you see it at its previous position −u―Tp, where it was positioned at the previous time −Tp. We can use the following figure to find the retarded position and time at which the light was emitted, then use this to find the velocity of the light.

To find the propagated distance of the light, we first have to derive the propagation time. You can skip past this derivation if you would like, as it does not add much to the understanding.

The triangle that the three vectors make in the diagram above allows us to get the equation for the velocity of the light as

(5.13)c―Tp=u―Tp+l―

with l―=(lx,ly,lz), writing out the vectors and rearranging to get the velocity vector for the light, gives

(5.14)c―=1Tp(lxlylz+uTp)

The magnitude of the light's displacement is equal to the distance the light travels in the corresponding propagation time cTp=‖c―Tp‖. The square of this gives

(5.15)(cTp)2=‖c―Tp‖2=(lx2+ly2+lz2)+u2Tp2+2uTplz,

rearranging this, we get the quadratic

(5.16)Tp2−(2γ2uc2lz)Tp−γ2c2(lx2+ly2+lz2)=0,

where γ=1/1−u2/c2. Now taking the positive solution to this, which corresponds to the past time, and making use of the identity

(5.17)γ2=1+γ2u2c2,

we get the result

(5.18)Tp=γ2uc2lz+(−γ2uc2lz)2+γ2c2(lx2+ly2+lz2)=γ2uc2lz+γclx2+ly2+(1+γ2u2c2)lz2=γ2uc2lz+γclx2+ly2+γ2lz2

This is the time it has taken to propagate the light from where the source was when it was emitted to the current position.

The propagated distance of the light can then be found from the derived propagation time, as

(5.19)Lp=cTp=γ2uclz+γL=γ(1+ucγlzL)L

With L=lx2+ly2+γ2lz2.

Substituting this into equation (5.14), we can find the light's velocity at l― to be

(5.20)c―=cγ(1+ucγlzL)(lxLlyLγ(γlzL+uc))

If we remove the speed of light from this light's velocity, we obtain its unit vector, with its z-component equal to the cosine of the angle from the z-axis, in this frame with the source moving, giving an equation that will come in useful in the next chapter:

(5.21)cos⁡α=γlzL+uc1+ucγlzL

Earlier, in the derivation above, you may have noticed that we introduced the γ term. Even though we are not changing frames and we are just looking at the delay in the signal that light has in reaching a particular point. We have made use of the γ term to simplify the equations as we do in special relativity, but we are not invoking special relativity here. I just wanted to emphasize that the γ term plays a role to here too, and it has to be this way to ensure special relativity is self-consistent when switching between frames. We will be looking at this when switching between frames in the next section.

5.7 Light's Propagation when switching from Rest Frame

This section is similar to what we just did, but here we will switch between frames, and that is where the emphasis will be. This section will be used in the next chapter when we have continuous pulses of light in all directions from a source and want to see how this field of light transforms and what it looks like with a moving source.

Here, we will look at the propagation of light that had been emitted from a source at rest, then switch to a frame where the source is now moving, using the Lorentz transformation of the emitted light's current locations in the rest frame (from r―0 to r―), but remembering these Lorentz transformed times t are not synchronized with the source's time of zero. So, we will use the moving frame's velocity of light, c―, to propagate back the light from where it is at time t to where it is at the origin's time of zero.


Now to derive the light's position at time of zero in the moving frame, l―

As visualized in figure (5.7) above. If we have a source in its rest frame that had emitted light from the origin and propagated to its current position r―0 at time t0=0. Then using the coordinate transform from equation (2.37) on position r―0=l―0=(l0x,l0y,l0z) with time t0=0, we get

(5.22)r―=(l0xl0yγl0z),at time: t=−γvc2l0z=γuc2l0z

The light's velocity in the moving frame can be found by using the velocity transform from equation (5.4) and converting the spherical polar coordinate to Cartesian using equation (5.1), giving

(5.23)c―=cγ(1+ucl0z‖l―0‖)(l0x‖l―0‖l0y‖l―0‖γ(l0z‖l―0‖+uc))

Now we have enough to find the position l― at which the light is when its time is synchronized with the source. We could use the triangle in figure (5.7.b), as we did in the previous section, which gives l―=c―Tp−u―Tp. But it is easier to use the Lorentz transformed position and time, and then propagate the light back to the time of zero, which is what we did in equation (5.12).

(5.24)l―=r―−c―t=(l0xl0yγl0z)−ucl0z1+ucl0z‖l―0‖(l0x‖l―0‖l0y‖l―0‖γ(l0z‖l―0‖+uc))=11+ucl0z‖l―0‖(l0x+ucl0z‖l―0‖l0x−ucl0zl0x‖l―0‖l0y+ucl0z‖l―0‖l0y−ucl0zl0y‖l―0‖γl0z+γucl0z‖l―0‖l0z−ucl0zγ(l0z‖l―0‖+uc))

Finally we can cancel out terms and simplify to get

(5.25)l―=11+ucl0z‖l―0‖(l0xl0y1γl0z)at time t=0

This is the position of the light at time zero, the same as the time of the source at the origin. This equation is what we will use to transform the positions of light in the next chapter, when we look at light being continuously emitted from a source, as shown in figure (6.1).

5.8 Summary

In this chapter, we looked at the equations for spherical polar coordinates and, with them, we derived the transform for the velocity of light. We used it to show that the emitted light is angled more towards the direction of a moving source relative than in the source's rest frame, a phenomenon known as relativistic aberration. We also showed that the frequency increases in the direction of motion relative to its rest frame, a phenomenon known as the Doppler effect. Together, these two effects are called relativistic beaming. After this, we looked at emitted light at time t0=0 in the source's rest frame, and how to transform it to a frame where the source is moving, to a time t=0. What we have learned will all come in useful in the next chapter, when we look at a source that continuously emits light in all directions and how this field of light transforms to a frame in which the source is moving.

Chapter 6. A Point Source: Continuously Emitting Light

This chapter will examine a source that, in its rest frame, continuously emits evenly distributed pulses of light. It gives a "field" of light, as shown in the first diagram in figure (6.1), with the second diagram in the figure showing how this "field" of light would look in a frame where the source is now moving. Equation (5.25) was used to transform each part of the propagating light to where it is at time t=0 (the time that it is synchronized with the source at the origin). The third diagram in the figure shows the rings for each pulse from a moving source. The Doppler effect in each direction is seen in how compact the rings are in each direction, with the aberrational effect on each ring shown by how the light is spread out on it. This combination of the relativistic Doppler and aberration effects together is called relativistic beaming.


Now that we have the means to transform this "field" of light, we can examine some of its physical/mathematical properties by considering each property in its rest frame and then determining how it extends to a frame in which it is moving. But first, we will look at how to describe an infinitesimal element on the surface of each spherical pulse. With this infinitesimal element, we will see how the density of the light on each pulse's surface changes when we look at a moving source, along with the Doppler effects on the density of light in the radial direction.

6.1 Surface Element on a Sphere and its Solid Angle

We will again return to spherical polar coordinates, but this time we will look at the differential elements used to describe an infinitesimal surface area on a sphere and, in turn, find out what a solid angle is and how to derive it. We can then find the density of light within this solid angle element. Then, using what we have learned previously about the aberration of light, we can find how this density of light changes for the case of a moving source.

So if we define a sphere with radius r, we can find an infinitesimal portion of the surface of the sphere at angles θ and ϕ as shown in this figure:

The surface element of a sphere at a constant radius r, spanning from θ to θ+dθ and ϕ to ϕ+dϕ, is equivalent to a rectangle with sides rdr and rsin⁡θdϕ giving the surface area as

(6.1)dA=r2sin⁡θdθdϕ

This surface element's size depends on the angle from the z-axis and the distance from the origin, but if we want a quantity that depends only on the angle, we can divide the surface element by r2; this gives what is called the solid angle. The solid angle element dΩ is a measure of the amount of the field of view, from the origin, that the surface element covers. For the differential surface element shown in the figure, we have the differential solid angle

(6.2)dΩ=dAr2=sin⁡θdθdϕ

If we were to integrate this over the whole sphere ∫02π∫0πsin⁡ϕdθdϕ, we would get 4π, which is when the surface fully covers the view from the origin. Therefore, the fraction of the view from the origin that is covered by a solid angle Ω is Ω/4π.

6.2 Surface Element's Light Density

Here we shall derive the light's density over an infinitesimal surface area perpendicular to the light's propagation, for a moving source. We will do this by first finding the density of light in the solid angle element for a moving source relative to the corresponding solid angle in the rest frame, then multiplying by the dissipation factor to get the density for the surface element, which is the inverse square of the propagated distance of the light from where it was emitted.

If we have a source at rest emitting light in all directions, we can say that at certain angles given by the spherical polar coordinates θ=α0 and ϕ=φ0, we have a quantity dQ of the emitted light's wavefront that is encompassed in the infinitesimal solid angle

(6.3)dΩ0=sin⁡α0dα0dφ0,

This is the same amount of the light's wavefront that is encompassed by the coinciding solid angle in the moving frame

(6.4)dΩ=sin⁡αdαdφ.

We can calculate this element by differentiating both sides of equation (5.5) with respect to α0 [7], which, after doing so, gives

(6.5)sin⁡αdα=1γ2(1+uccos⁡α0)2sin⁡α0dα0

now using this and dφ=dφ0 (as the angle φ0 is always perpendicular to the motion of the particle and unaffected by the transformation), we have the solid angle in the moving frame given as

(6.6)dΩ=1γ2(1+uccos⁡α0)2sin⁡α0dα0dφ0.

If there is the same quantity of light dQ in the solid angle element in both frames, then the density of light in the solid angle in each frame is dQ/dΩ0 and dQ/dΩ respectively, giving the ratio of the density in the solid angle element in the moving frame relative to the rest frame as

(6.7)Dσ=dΩ0dΩ=γ2(1+uccos⁡α0)2.

By substituting equation (5.21) into equation (5.6), we get cos⁡α0=γlzL, which allows us to get this in terms of the light's position in its moving frame

(6.8)Dσ=γ2(1+ucγlzL)2.

with L=lx2+ly2+γ2lz2.

Dσ is the density of light in a solid angle element for a moving source relative to the density of light in the corresponding solid angle element in the rest frame of the source.

At position (lx,ly,lz), light has propagated a distance Lp from where it was emitted, given in equation (5.19). Its surface area element grows by a factor of Lp2, and the light's density in a surface element's area dissipates by the inverse of this:

(6.9)1Lp2=1γ2(1+ucγlzL)2L2

Multiplying this by the density of light in the solid angle element relative to the rest source, Dσ/Lp2, we get the density of light in the surface element given as

(6.10)Dσ=kσL2with L=lx2+ly2+γ2lz2

Where kσ is the proportionality constant.

For a source at rest, u=0, we have γ=1, and this equation then gives the inverse square of the distance from the rest source, as

(6.11)Dσ=kσlx2+ly2+lz2

This inverse square law is what we will get when setting u=0 for all the properties of the light field that we will look at in each section.

1L2 will appear several times in this chapter for a moving source, and is plotted below for a moving source and a source at rest.

6.3 Density in the direction of propagation of light

For the case where light is being continuously emitted from a source at rest, as shown in figure (6.1.a), the light is emitted from the stationary source at a constant rate. Because of this constant rate of emission from the rest source, the light has no change in density in the direction of the light's propagation.

The Doppler effect gives the frequency of light from a moving source relative to its rest frame, in which it is constant. The change in density of light in its propagation direction is inversely proportional to this change in frequency,

Since this density is constant for a stationary source. Then we have this density for a moving source proportional to the Doppler effect from equation (5.10), which we can get in our current frame's coordinates by substituting in equation (5.21), giving this density for a moving source to be

(6.12)Dc=γ(1+ucγlzL)kc

Where kc is the constant density of light in the direction of the light's propagation for a stationary source.

6.4 Coordinates used

Previously, we had used a separate notation for the source's rest frame. In this chapter, we will not switch between frames; we will remain in the same frame and change the source's speed u instead. The speed will be set to zero, u=0, to look at the case of a source at rest. We will therefore use the same notation for position coordinates throughout this chapter: (x,y,z).

We will be substituting these coordinates into equations from previous sections, for the position of light in the moving frame

(6.13)l―=(lx,ly,lz)=(x,y,z)

I hope this will not lead to confusion, since we previously used a separate notation for the source's rest frame.

6.5 Volume Density of Light

Here, we will see what the volume density of light is for a moving source. We have the densities of light in the direction of its propagation, Dc, and in the plane perpendicular to it, Dσ, given by equations (6.10) and (6.12).

Giving the volume density to be

(6.14)D=DσDc=γ(1+ucγzL)kσkcL2

This density of light for a moving source at any point is shown in the following diagram: the left figure shows the volume density of light emitted from a source at rest when u=0, demonstrating the inverse square law.

This summary has been left as an exercise for the reader to fill in.

Part IV.
Conclusion and Resources

Chapter 7. Conclusion

This handbook of special relativity has gone through a lot. However, there is still plenty I have yet to distill, and I will hopefully include more sections when I get the time. For now, I hope this handbook was useful to you. If you are still looking for more in the meantime, there are plenty of external resources in chapter (8) to expand your knowledge and give you some different perspectives and mental practice.

I will leave you with a final note on gravity and its role in relativity.

7.1 A Note on Gravity

For a reference frame to be inertial there has to be zero acceleration, but the gravity of the earth and other masses accelerates objects towards them. Out in space, we still have this acceleration even though it may be weak, so special relativity can actually only be used as an approximation when modeling a system. Where gravity is stronger or time scales are much longer and these approximations are not good enough, we require an even more complex view of the world and the next level of frame transformations, between two non-inertial frames of reference. This is where general relativity comes in. It is used to explain the redshift of light from stars and also the bending of light around massive stars. It also explains the difference in the flow of time at different strengths of gravity; this gravitational time dilation has to be taken into account by the satellites used by GPS systems. But there are downsides to general relativity, such as its incompatibility with quantum mechanics, its failure to explain why galaxies rotate much faster than they should based on the visible matter, and its failure to explain why the expansion of the universe is accelerating. It requires inventing new invisible entities to explain these, called dark matter and dark energy (which are vague concepts, as they are whatever new particles or physics are invented that happen to describe some of the discrepancy in the gravity well enough). However, these concepts still fail in many cases. There is also a competitor theory called MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics). While it clears up some discrepancies, it fails in many other instances.

So the correct theory and full description of gravity is still to be decided.

But if you want to start learning more about gravity, the thought experiment that started general relativity is undeniably a perfect starting point.

7.1.1 Elevator Thought Experiment and the Equivalence Principle

If you were in an elevator in free fall, you would feel weightless, as you would also be free-falling at the same speed, and feel no force from the floor of the elevator into your feet, just like the springs feel no force in the inertial frame in the first diagram of Figure (1.3). You would also feel the same weightlessness if you were in an elevator out in deep space, away from any masses. Even though someone at rest on earth would see you accelerating towards the ground in the free-falling elevator, you would not be able to tell the difference between these two situations from inside the windowless elevators, i.e., the reference frames of both elevators are equivalent. The free-falling elevator feels as though it is at rest or in an inertial frame of reference.

Now, what about an elevator at rest on earth? If a ball is dropped from rest, as shown in figure (7.1), it has an acceleration of g downwards.

Now, what if we apply the same acceleration to the elevator in deep space? In an inertial frame outside the elevator we would see the elevator accelerate towards the ball, as shown in figure (7.2.a). But inside the elevator, in its non-inertial frame, we would see the ball accelerate towards the elevator floor at the same acceleration as the elevator at rest on earth, as shown in figure (7.2.a). You would also feel the same weight on your feet. Again, the frames of both of these elevators are equivalent.


So the mass released from rest behaves identically whether the elevator is accelerating upwards in deep space at g or sitting stationary on the surface of the earth experiencing a gravitational pull of g.

Formally, the gravitational equivalence principle states that there is no local physical experiment you can perform to distinguish between being in a uniform gravitational field and being in a uniformly accelerating reference frame.

Let us now see how this equivalence allows us to deduce that gravity bends the path of light.

If we are in an inertial reference frame outside the elevator in deep space, and shine a light horizontally through a hole in the elevator, it will travel in a straight line across the elevator in this inertial frame. But the elevator is accelerating, and as the light moves across, the elevator rises up more and more quickly, and the light hits the other side of the elevator at a lower point, as shown in figure (7.3.a). From the non inertial frame, inside the elevator, we would see the path of light bend downwards and hit the wall at the lower point, as shown in figure (7.3.a).


The light's path is bent in the non inertial frame, but from the equivalence principle, the frame inside an elevator at rest on earth is equivalent, since it experiences the same acceleration due to gravity. So we would then expect to find that gravity does, in fact, bend the light by the same amount, shown in figure (7.4). This has been experimentally verified: light does indeed bend around heavy masses such as stars, black holes, and to a lesser extent, planets.

In the real world, the gravitational field in the elevator on earth is not perfectly uniform, but it is a good approximation. The top of the elevator is further from earth and so gravity is a slightly weaker than at the bottom. Also, for a spherical mass, the gravitational field spreads out spherically, creating a negligible difference in the gravitational strength in the center of the elevator compared to the walls; this is called a tidal force. These are negligible effects for our thought experiment, but might be significant when modeling other systems.

In general relativity, the local speed of light is always equal to c according to the observer who is there. But when viewed from a different gravitational strength, it appears to be moving at a different speed. This effect is tied to gravitational time dilation, which we will give a note about next.

7.1.2 Gravitational Time Dilation

We have seen the time dilation equation in special relativity between two reference frames, but gravity also has a time dilation associated with its strength. The stronger the gravity at a point, the slower time passes relative to an inertial reference frame that doesn't experience any gravitational force.

(7.1)Δtg=Δt∞1−vesc2c2

Where vesc is the minimum velocity an object has to be traveling away from a mass to escape its orbit, and Δtg is the change in time within a gravitational well compared to the change in time at an infinite distance away Δt∞. This is the same as the time dilation in special relativity as seen in equation (2.15) if we were to use v=vesc. The escape velocity is also the same velocity (but in the opposite direction) that a particle would have if it started at rest an infinite distance away and reached the current position in a stationary mass's gravitational field. There is an interpretation of general relativity called the "river model" [8], which suggests that gravity and its effects are due to space itself falling inwards at this velocity at each point. It also extended this to rotating masses. This model is an interpretation that can be useful for learning general relativity, but it is a niche interpretation. So, you can keep an open mind about it and remain skeptical about whether the interpretation is worthwhile.

This concludes The Handbook of Special Relativity, but please check out the other resources on this topic that I have provided in the next bit.

Chapter 8. Resources

Here are some useful resources for learning different aspects of special relativity, including spacetime diagrams which I choose not to use as a learning aid in this handbook.

There is one thing that you should take into account when using these resources compared to this handbook, and that is that in this handbook we have chosen for the primed frame to be moving in the z-direction throughout, as it was needed when in came to spherical coordinates, whereas it is more common to have the primed frame going in the x-direction. So you just need to swap the x and z coordinates in transformation equations to get the same transformations.

Chapter 9. Definitions

Mathematical Framework

Reference frame: An abstract coordinate system, consisting of three spatial and one time axis. The origin, orientation, and scale of its axis are specified by a set of points in space. The purpose of it is to provide a standardized means of defining the position and orientation of objects at any instant in time.
Inertial reference frame: A reference frame that is not undergoing any acceleration. An observer's reference frame is inertial if they do not feel a force acting on them.
Proper/Rest frame: This is the reference frame of the observer or object itself.
Primed frame: A reference frame that is moving relative to the current frame.
Initial frame: The first reference frame that we are comparing the current or primed reference frame to.
Moving frame: An inertial reference frame that is moving relative to the rest frame.
frame velocity: The velocity of a reference frame relative to the current reference frame.
Frame transform: The changing of coordinates and other quantities in a reference frame into their corresponding values in another reference frame.
Galilean/Classical frame transform: Transformation of coordinates and physical quantities according to Newtonian physics between two frames of reference.
Relativistic frame transform: The changing of the spatial coordinates, the time coordinate, and other physical quantities into their corresponding values in a different inertial reference frame using equations from special relativity.
Observer: An entity/thing with an associated frame of reference/system of coordinates, with respect to which you can measure an object's position, orientation, shape, signal emission and other properties.
Event: An occurrence that can be specified by a unique combination of the three spatial and one time coordinates. These four coordinates, together, form a point in spacetime.
Simultaneity: Within a reference frame, two or more events are simultaneous if they occur at the same time within it. Classically, if any two events are simultaneous in one reference frame, they are also simultaneous in another. This is not true in special relativity, and the order of events can depend on the frame of reference.
Retarded position: The previous position of a source, that an observer/reciever currently sees it at, due to the time delay between when a moving source emitting a light signal and when the observer/reciever detects it.
Retarded time: The previous time when a source was at its retarded position (the position it emitted the light signal that is curently being observered by the observer).
Retarded coordinates: The retarded positions of an initial reference frame's coordinates within a second reference frame, at thier retarded times.

The Mechanics

Aether: A proposed medium that filled the vacuum of space that light propagated through.
Vacuum: Space that contains no matter.
Lorentz length contraction: The shortening of a moving object along the direction of its motion relative to an observer (compared to the length of object at rest).
Time dilation: The slowing of the passing of time for objects in motion relative to an observer, compared to the passing of time for the observer.
Doppler effect: The change of a wave's frequency due to the motion of its source relative to an observer. This is due to the bunching up of the wave in the direction of movement of the source and the stretching of the wave in the opposite direction, as well as the dilation of time between the emission of the crests of the emitted wave.
Aberration of light: The changing of the direction of the propagation of light when changing to another reference frame.
Relativistic beaming: The accumulation of the Doppler effect and aberration of light, and how it affects the amount of light and its frequency emitted at different angles from a moving source. This effect can be extended to any wave or field emitted at the speed of light from a moving source.
Retarded field: A moving source's field, where each point in the field has had its field propagated at the speed of light from the source's retarded position (i.e. the previous position of the source where it had emitted that part of the field from).
Field: A physical quantity that has a value (or a set of values) assigned to every point in space and time.
Light year: The distance light travels in one year (in a vacuum).

Definitions for Later Chapters

Lorentz Invariant/Frame independent: A quantity or law of physics is Lorentz Invariant/Frame independent, if it remains unchanged when transforming coordinates and other quantities to any other inertial reference frame.
Postulates: A statement that is assumed to be true and is used as a basis for reasoning for a theory.
Flux: A measure of how much of a quantity is passing through a given surface in a given time (flowrate through a surface)
Perceived/Apparent Velocity: The velocity an object appears to have due to the time delay in the signal of light from it, as the time delay from each position along a sources path is different due to having different distances the signal needs to travel to observer (It is the consequence of the time difference in the propagation time of the light signal from the different positions of a source's path).
Rest mass: The mass of a particle in its own rest frame.
Rest mass energy: The energy a particle has due to its rest mass (given by its rest mass times speed of light squared).

The previous time when a source was at its retarded position (the position it emitted the light signal that is curently being observered by the observer).
Retarded coordinates:
The retarded positions of an initial reference frame's coordinates within a second reference frame, at thier retarded times.
Aether:
A proposed medium that filled the vacuum of space that light propagated through.
Vacuum:
Space that contains no matter.
Lorentz length contraction:
The shortening of a moving object along the direction of its motion relative to an observer (compared to the length of object at rest).
Time dilation:
The slowing of the passing of time for objects in motion relative to an observer, compared to the passing of time for the observer.
Doppler effect:
The change of a wave's frequency due to the motion of its source relative to an observer. This is due to the bunching up of the wave in the direction of movement of the source and the stretching of the wave in the opposite direction, as well as the dilation of time between the emission of the crests of the emitted wave.
Aberration of light:
The changing of the direction of the propagation of light when changing to another reference frame.
Relativistic beaming:
The accumulation of the Doppler effect and aberration of light, and how it affects the amount of light and its frequency emitted at different angles from a moving source. This effect can be extended to any wave or field emitted at the speed of light from a moving source.
Retarded field:
A moving source's field, where each point in the field has had its field propagated at the speed of light from the source's retarded position (i.e. the previous position of the source where it had emitted that part of the field from).
Field:
A physical quantity that has a value (or a set of values) assigned to every point in space and time.
Light year:
The distance light travels in one year (in a vacuum).
Lorentz Invariant/Frame independent:
A quantity or law of physics is Lorentz Invariant/Frame independent, if it remains unchanged when transforming coordinates and other quantities to any other inertial reference frame.
Postulates:
A statement that is assumed to be true and is used as a basis for reasoning for a theory.
Flux:
A measure of how much of a quantity is passing through a given surface in a given time (flowrate through a surface)
Perceived/Apparent Velocity:
The velocity an object appears to have due to the time delay in the signal of light from it, as the time delay from each position along a sources path is different due to having different distances the signal needs to travel to observer (It is the consequence of the time difference in the propagation time of the light signal from the different positions of a source's path).
Rest mass:
The mass of a particle in its own rest frame.
Rest mass energy:
The energy a particle has due to its rest mass (given by its rest mass times speed of light squared).
